subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In rising to make some observations in regard to the national budget which was presented to this house on Friday last by the Minister of Finance, let me in the first place congratulate my hon. friend the minister on the lucidity of his annual statement upon the present occasion. Let me also congratulate 7S594-474
him upon the precision of his language in regard to certain important announcements which he made in his address to this house, and also upon the concise manner in which he laid the financial transactions of Canada before us. Subject to some observations which I may have occasion to make later on, let me say that we on this side of the house rejoice with those in every other quarter of the house that Providence has continued to shower upon this country unbounded prosperity; and if we on this side are inclined to attribute the major portion of the credit for this happy condition of affairs to a beneficent Providence and to the intelligence and industry of our people rather than to the government little surprise will be felt that we take this attitude. Indeed, on occasions of this kind, one is inclined to speculate how much greater, how much wider and how much more evenly distributed that prosperity might have been in this country had we in power in Canada today a government more fully alive to the possibilities of this great country, and to the rights and interests of every class of the citizens of this Dominion.
Personally I express my own satisfaction that the Minister of Finance on this occasion has given' us a clearer and, if I may say so without offence, a much more candid statement of our financial affairs than was his wont on former occasions. And I state also my personal opinion that the statistical information which he has laid before parliament on this occasion will probably serve to remove from discussion some at least of the controversial points of previous discussions.
I think we may now take it as fairly well settled that the net debt of the Dominion of Canada on March 31 next will be the sum of $2,227,068,000, as stated by the Minister of Finance. This has always been a more or less controversial point. We have never had very serious controversy about the funded debt of the country, but I am glad to note that in his speech last Friday the minister for the first time took serious account of what we know as the funded or bonded debt or, as he put it in his remarks, the dead weight debt of the Dominion of Canada. That, after all, is the important item in the financing of this country. The net debt is not a matter of the greatest consequence; in England they never refer to it at all. There they use the One term "dead weight debt", and I am glad that the minister has used that term on this occasion, because that is the debt which counts. It is the amount for which the government of this country has issued in solemn form its bonds and obliga-
The Budget-Mr. Guthrie

tions, signed, sealed and delivered, which bonds are now held by people who have invested in our securities. These bonds have to be paid at maturity, and in the meantime interest must be met. They therefore constitute the real burden which the people of this country are compelled to carry.
The net debt is comparatively unimportant; it is a matter very largely of bookkeeping and depends upon how you see fit to estimate the value of your assets. We have assets that are certainly good liquid assets, but we have a lot of assets in this country which we carry as non-active assets, and if you want to transfer some of these non-active assets to the active list you can immediately decrease your net debt. It is, I say, a matter largely of bookkeeping. But the debt which counts is the dead weight debt.
Now we may take it from the statement of the minister that the dead weight debt in this country, as of March 31 instant, will be the sum of $2,330,835,000. That dead weight debt stood on the books of Canada on March 31, 1922, when this government first assumed power, at $2,420,000,000. So that after seven years of financing by this government there is a reduction in the dead weight debt of Canada of $90,000,000, or an average reduction of $13,000,000 per annum since tlhe government took office.
Mr. Speaker, I consider an annual reduction of the dead weight debt of $13,000,000 a fairly substantial payment. I think that under all the circumstances it should have been more. But I am not altogether dissatisfied with the reduction of $90,000,000 in seven years. I submit to the minister tha-t without further delay in this matter he should present a definite scheme to this house for the retirement of the whole of the dead weight debt. Every year for the past three or four years this question has been brought to the attention of the minister. Year after year he has evaded it; he has said nothing to the house respecting it, although last year, I believe, he did allege that some man named McCulloch, writing on financial questions in England some eighty years ago, had declared that the system of payment of debts by way of sinking fund was unsound. That is the only reason the Finance minister has given the house for his refusal to adopt a definite scheme for the retirement of our debt. I can only tell my hon. friend the Minister of Finance that the government of Great Britain, in spite of Mr. McCulloch's language, has adopted a definite scheme of debt retirement; they have done so in France; they have done so in the United States in regard to their war debt and 
they have done so in the province of Ontario in regard to the provincial debt. In each of these instances in thirty, forty or fifty years as the case may be these dead weight debts will be paid off. It was pointed out last year in this house by my leader that if the Minister of Finance would appropriate out of his enormous revenues the sum of $19,000,000 a year as a sinking fund, even with interest at only 4 per cent in forty-five years the accumulation of this fund would pay the whole of the dead weight debt of this country; or if $19,000,000 per annum is too much-and I submit it is not-if he took the sum of $15,000,000 per year, in fifty years we would wipe out the dead weight debt of Canada.
There is much to commend such a step to any reasonable man in this proposal. In the first place a system of that kind enhances the credit of the country in the financial centres of the world. When you go to the money markets of the world and the money lenders find that you have established a definite system of debt retirement by means of sinking funds, your credit is enhanced immediately. The province of Ontario has found this to be so in the New York market; they can now borrow money in New York on their bonds more cheaply than was the case formerly. We could do the same for the Dominion, and thus enhance our national credit. This was done in Great Britain, and while there never was a doubt about British credit yet they have re-established that credit in the eyes of the world on a firmer basis than ever before. We could do so also.
But there is still a further element worth considering in this connection. A definite commitment of $15,000,000 or $19,000,000 a year to be taken from the treasury for the payment of funded debt would prevent the accumulation of an unnecessary amount of money in the treasury, which is always a great temptation to a minister, to a government or to a private individual to relax anything in the nature of economic principles, and a great temptation to indulge in a course of extravagant expenditure. The adoption of such a system, which would permit us annually to take from our treasury a definite sum of money, would act as a serious check upon the spending propensities of the present government, and I trust the Minister of Finance will seriously consider this matter and next session bring in some plan which may be adopted by the house in regard to this question.
Now I pass on to the surplus announced this year by the minister, a surplus which in some respects is very creditable. A surplus

The Budget-Mr. Guthrie
in this country is arrived at in a prosperous year very simply; all the receipts of the government go into a single fund known as the consolidated revenue fund; all payments for the management of the business of the country are made from that fund. If the receipts are greater than the expenditures in any year there is a surplus, and if the expenditures exceed the receipts there is a deficit. This year the minister has announced a surplus of $99,000,000, out of which he proposes to pay in capital charges and special expenditure the sum of $29,000,000, leaving in round figures a net surplus of $69,000,000, with which he says he has reduced, or on March 31 next will be able to reduce, the net debt of this country by at least $50,000,000. For some reason best known to himself, when the Minister of Finance makes financial comparisons he studiously avoids any reference to the year 1923; he always starts his statements and comparisons with the year 1924, and his reason for so doing is purely artificial. He should start with the fiscal year 1923. Mr. Fielding was in control of the treasury then, and Mr. Fielding always assumed full responsibility for the financing of Canada during the year 1923. The Minister of Finance has announced that from the year 1924 to the year 1929, inclusive, he has been able to reduce the national debt by the sum of $226,000,000, or an average annual reduction of $37,700,000. Had he included the year 1923, as he should have done, his average reduction per annum would have fallen from $37,700,000 to $27,860,000, but because the year 1923 was not a very favourable year in Dominion financing, in all or nearly all "the statements of the present Minister of Finance he deliberately excludes that year from his calculation.
In the year 1923 and in the year 1922 we had to add to the debt of this country. We had surpluses in those years, just as the minister has surpluses now, but perhaps it would be as well for Mr. Fielding himself to explain the financing of those two years. Those who heard him make his financial statement in this house on June 10, 1923, will recall his language; speaking then of the fiscal year 1922, which closed on March 31, 1923, he would have nothing to do with it although he was Minister of Finance during 1922. but he assumed full responsibility for the following fiscal year 1923. Well, he closed the year 1922 with a pretty handsome surplus, amounting to $34,000.000; out of this surplus he paid capital charges and special expenditures amounting to $18,000,000, so he closed that year with an actual cash surplus of $16,000,000. Then, however, he was met with deficits and cash
requirements on the part of the national railways and the merchant marine; that year these demanded from him a sum of no less than $97,000,000. He had only $16,000,000 of surplus in the treasury, and consequently had to borrow money to make up these railway deficits, and in doing so increased the debt of Canada for that year by $81,000,000. The following year practically the same thing happened; he closed the year with a surplus of $62,000,000 in the treasury, which is a fairly substantial amount. He paid all the capital and special charges, amounting to $24,500,000, leaving a balance in cash of $37,500,000. However, war demobilization, the merchant marine and the national railways again demanded the sum of $68,000,000, so instead of having a cash surplus of $37,500,000 that year he added to the debt of the country by $31,000,000, and it is by reason of that addition to the debt in 1923 that the present Minister of Finance carefully excludes that year from all his calculations
Mr. Fielding did just what his predecessors in office had done. When there were deficits with respect to the Canadian National Railways; when money had to be supplied them for other purposes as well as deficits he put his hand in the treasury, took out the money and paid the charges and charged them to the debt of Canada. After Mr. Fielding's time, however, a change took place and we entered upon a new era of railway financing. I do not say that the new scheme is not good and sound; in fact I prefer it to the old scheme. Under the new scheme railway finances are kept separate as far as possible, whereas under the former government and in Mr. Fielding's time the treasury stood all the losses, and these losses were added to the debt of Canada. The railway now issues its own bonds and the government of Canada guarantees them by endorsement on the back of the bond instead of, as in the old days, signing the front of the bond. That is practically the only difference in the two systems, but it makes an enormous difference with regard to the financial accounts and statements of the Dominion of Canada. The Minister of Finance announced a surplus of $99,000,000 for the past year's operations, and of course there was tremendous applause from the government benches when that announcement wa3 made. But let me say, Mr. Speaker, that the record of this government, starting with the year 1923 up to the present year inclusive, is scarcely one whit better than the record of its predecessor. The public accounts of this country disclose the fact, astonishing to some people, that the surpluses under the

The aggregate for these years amounts to about $487,812,000, or an average per year of $69,687,000, or just about $3,000,000 more per year of surplus under the Liberal government than was the case under the Conservative government which preceded it. I make that statement largely in view of the fact that during the present session the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) flourished the public accounts in our faces when we were discussing the building of national highways. He referred to the fact that during the years I have enumerated, under the Conservatives the debt of this countrj' had been materially increased. That was a most misleading statement, and no one knows better than the Prime Minister that the increased debt of those years was due to two causes, and two causes only. During those years we had practically as large surpluses and spent far less money on consolidated fund account than has this government, but the acquisition of the 
Canadian National railway system and the conduct of Canada's part in the Great war accounted for the increased debt of the country. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the finances of the Canadian National railways are so inextricably interwoven with the finances of the Dominion of Canada that one cannot get a fair picture of either situation when viewing them separately. To a large extent they must be considered together and I am glad that the Minister of Finance has treated them in that way on this occasion. The interests of this country are deeply wrapped up in that great railway undertaking. It is by far the largest financial concern which this country has. Does the house realize just what it involves? I cannot give the precise figures with regard to the national railways for the year just closed, because the statement has not been issued, but I can take the financial statement of the preceding year as a basis and account for certain changes in figures which have occurred in the interval and which have come to the knowledge of the house.
I find that the Canadian National system had a bonded debt to private bondholders amounting to $981,000,000, as of January 1, 1928. According to the statement made to this house by the Minister of Finance, this year the bonded indebtedness will be increased by the sum of $44,000,000. These figures disclose the fact that the bonded indebtedness of the Canadian National railway system to the public has now passed the billion dollar mark. What about the Dominion of Canada's interest in that system? On January 1, 1928, Canada was a creditor of that system to the extent of $1,258,000,000; the total indebtedness of the road as of that date was $2,239,000,000. I give these figures in order that we may understand the tremendous financial undertaking in which we are involved in regard to these national railways. The result of operations for last year was very gratifying, and I would ask the Minister of Finance to note that the treasury of this country has been relieved very substantially for the last four or five years through the successful operation of Canada's national railway system. On January 1, 1924, an announcement was made by the president that for the first time in its history the national system had produced a net revenue over operating expenses, for the year 1923, amounting to $4,155,000; in 1924 that revenue had increased to $18,000,000; in
1925	it had increased again to $33,000,000; in
1926	the revenue was $48,000,000; in 1927 it dropped back to $42,000,000; and for 1928 we have the wonderful result of a surplus in net operating expenses amounting to $58,000,000.

The Budget-Mr. Guthrie
It will take $50,000,000 of that amount to pay the interest on the bonds which the public hold, I understand the management of the road will pay that interest this year and will still have on hand a balance of $8,000,000 for other purposes. But what about the money it owes to the Dominion treasury? The minister intimates that the sum of $32,000,000 odd is owed this year to the government for interest. It is put down in the books as a debt of the railway but is purely a bookkeeping transaction and I presume it will be added to the $1,258,000,000 which the company owed to us at the beginning of the year, making the total indebtedness of the system to the Dominion treasury about $1,300,000,000 and to the public about $1,000,000,000.
In respect, however, to the national railway we on this side of the house are all optimists. We look upon that railway as practically our own infant and our own creature. Those of us who were in parliament-it is perhaps pretty far back-in the early days prior to 1911 know there was great activity in railway building in this country in those years. We far outbuilt the requirements of the Dominion of Canada as they existed at that time, but personally I am not in a position to offer any criticism whatever of the railway undertakings of those days because I was one of those who supported the proposals. However, early in the years of the war something in the nature of a national catastrophe was imminent to the Dominion of Canada in respect of our railways. The very extensive system known as the Canadian Northern, with all its subsidiaries and all its ramifications, became seriously involved financially. The government had to come to its rescue to the extent of an enormous amount of money and the only security which we could obtain from the Canadian Northern system was a blanket mortgage upon the whole undertaking and a transfer of sufficient of the shares in the various companies to give the government control of the whole undertaking. Apart from the granting of substantial aid, financial disaster loomed ahead of us. The Grand Trunk Pacific came next; insolvency stood at the door of that railway; the road was in fact insolvent. In that case * we went to the exchequer court and asked that the affairs of the Grand Trunk Pacific be taken from the management which was then the old Grand Trunk company, and that it be placed in the hands of a receiver. It was placed in the hands of the Minister of Railways of Canada as receiver. No sooner had these matters been temporarily arranged than the financial difficulties of the old Grand
Trunk railway system became only too apparent. That road was absolutely insolvent. Canada was threatened with railway insolvency on every hand. Moreover, across the ocean in France and Flanders we were carrying on Canada's part in the greatest war in history. There was serious financial calamity awaiting us at home unless speedy action was taken to relieve the railway situation and at the same time hundreds of millions of dollars had to be supplied to carry on the war. Such then was the critical situation in this country in the years 1918 and 1919.
The leader of the government (Mr. Mackenzie King) was not, I think, in the house until September of the year 1919, when he was returned for a constituency in Prince Edward Island and came back to the house as leader of the Liberal party. But he was present in the house during the second session of 1919 and I recall with the greatest distinctness what transpired during that session. So will my right hon. friend; so will the Minister of Finance; so would the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) if he were in his place. A great fight was then waged by the Conservative party to take over these three railway systems that had gone into bankruptcy, reorganize them, consolidate them and make them into a Canadian National railway to be owned by the people of the Dominion of Canada. This was the only way to save the country from what might have been national bankruptcy. Indeed, in spite of what we did, the prediction of national bankruptcy was made in the city of Montreal by so great a financial authority as Sir Lomer Gouin and other prominent persons.
We had a bitter fight in the session of 1919 in the old museum building, where we then sat, but we were fortunate in that great fight to have a very brilliant man to lead our forces in regard to the railway problem. I refer to the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, who I believe was the first public man to realize the full gravity of the situation and who wa* at all times the great factor in engineering our way out of our railway difficulty. He formulated a definite plan; he produced it before parliament. It was immediately opposed in the bitterest manner by the Liberal party in the House of Commons, by the Liberal party in the Dominion of Canada and, I regret to say, by many friends and some newspapers otherwise friendly to the Conservative party. Mr. Meighen had a tremendous task ahead of him. Day in and day out in the old museum during the session of 1919 the railway bill was fought to a finish. Every kind and method of opposition was urged
The Budget-Mr. Guthrie

against it. Nothing was left undone or unsaid by our opponents. We were told that we were going to bankrupt the Dominion of Canada. It was claimed that those roads should be put into liquidation, go through the exchequer court of Canada and be put on the auction block. If such a course had been followed there was only one power in Canada to purchase them and that power would have been able to create the greatest railway monopoly ever created in any country in the world.
I remember some of the amendments that were moved on that occasion and I will mention one or two of them. Under the guidance of Mr. Meighen that bill was fought through the house. Amendment after amendment was moved to defeat it. The late Hon. D. D. McKenzie moved that the matter be dropped and not considered for the present time. His motion was defeated. Then came a motion by Mr. Denis, at that time member for Joliette and until recently a member of the house. His motion was defeated. Then there was a motion by the Right Hon. Mr. Fielding to appoint a royal commission to inquire into the whole matter, his object being to defeat the bill and to destroy the government as well. His motion was defeated. After that followed a motion by my right hon. friend the present Prime Minister on the third reading of the bill, just before it was passed, a motion to recommit it to the committee of the whole house, which constituted a want of confidence motion in the government on the third reading. It was intended to defeat the government and to destroy the bill. There followed another motion, which to-day seems rather ludicrous, moved by the hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Parent). I would like to recall to the house the amendment which he moved. On the third reading of the bill the member for Quebec West formally moved that in the opinion of the House of Commons, as the Grank Trunk railway had terminals in the United States, our taking this road over as a national undertaking would involve us in annexation to the United States. Such of course were not the exact words of the amendment but merely the sense of it. At this distance of time it would seem impossible that any man would vote for a proposal of that kind, yet in the division list I find the following names-King. Lapointe, and others. Our good friend the Minister of Finance was cute; he ducked that vote; his name does not even appear in the list of pairs. When the Liberals had exhausted every effort to beat us, when they had tried everything in their power to destroy that measure and prevent the nationalization of these railways, the present Minister of Finance was put up to lead the final attack, and in the early hours 
of the morning he solemnly moved that the bill be given the six months' hoist. Again I look at the division list, and I find amongst those who supported the six months' hoist to destroy that measure, the following names: King, Robb and Lapointe. Such was the attitude of the Liberal party at that time, and of the Liberal press, and also as I said before, of an influential part of the Conservative press of Canada. They were all mistaken, badly mistaken in their judgment. The Liberals tried by everything in their power to destroy that measure but they failed. With them it was a case of the spirit being willing, but the flesh was weak.

speechtext:
It may have been as my right hon. friend suggests, but I know that ninety per cent of the discussion at that session centered around the railway question. Two great volumes of Hansard are full of that discussion, and of little else. No, Mr. Speaker, hon. gentlemen opposite had no faith in a national railway system then, and they tried to kill it at its birth, and for two or three years afterwards they continued their efforts to destroy it. Why, even when the present government first obtained power, in the very first speech delivered from the throne, a speech penned by my right hon. friend the Prime Minister, he takes occasion in that speech to remark:
The transportation system weighs heavily upon our national finances.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That was right.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Certainly, that was true
in the early days, and it accounted for a very large part of the additions to the national debt, but even at that time my right hon. friend the prime minister had not become a convert either to the nationalization of the railways or to public ownership in general. He only took it on trial; in fact, it was popularly supposed by those outside the secrets of the cabinet that the system was going to be broken up, and not continued as a national

The Budget-Mr. Guthrie
undertaking. There were strong influences pulling the government this way, but other influences pulling them in the right direction, of course, and the government finally agreed just to feeling its way, and the Prime Minister made the Governor General say with great caution in the speech from the throne that he had decided "to give government ownership and operation a fair trial.''

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
A pretty good
decision.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, and a reluctant one, too. My object, Mr. Speaker, in going into these old matters is this: Now, when this wonderful Canadian National railway system has more than justified itself, now, that it is rapidly becoming in the nature of a great national asset, now that we may look forward to a day, not perhaps in my lifetime, but in the lifetime of some here, when this system will start repaying the government of Canada part at least of the money it owes to the treasury, to the day when it will have a clean sheet, as it ultimately will have, in regard to its bonded indebtedness to the public; now that the system is in this, a thoroughly prosperous condition, this government desires to treat it as its own creature. Whereas in 1919 it tried to cast it out as base-born, now it wants to consider it as its legitimate offspring, and to profit by its success. Let me say, in concluding my remarks on this phase of the subject, that the national railway system in this country constitutes a lasting monument to the ability and statesmanship and determination of a single man, a member of a former Conservative government, and subsequently Prime Minister of that government. It is to his ability and foresight, to his statesmanship and determination that the people of Canada are indebted for this wonderful system of national railways.
There is another question in the budget which I think we should carefully consider, and that is the question of the cost of government in this country. The cost of government in this country is going up so rapidly that it is now out of all proportion with the advances which the country has made either in business or in population. When this government first came into power, I grant that they endeavoured to make some effort to reduce expenditure. Mr. Fielding, I fancy, did his best in that direction. For the year 1923, according to the public accounts we spent 1350,000,000; in 1924, Mr. Fielding reduced that to $344,000,000; in 1925, he further reduced it to $339,000,000, and then, perhaps
unfortunately for the country he retired from office. His successor the present Finance minister came into office at a time when the annual expenditure was $339,000,000. The first year after he assumed office the expenditure jumped to $343,000,000; in 1927, to $346,000,000; in 1928, to $360,000,000, and for the year just closed, according to the minister's own figures on Friday last, the expenditure was $385,000,000. Starting with an annual expenditure of $339,000,000 when he took office in 1925, he has increased that expenditure to the enormous figure of $391,000,000 to-day, or an increase in a few short years of $52,000,000 in annual expenditure. The business of the country has not increased in that ratio; the population of the country has not increased in that ratio; conditions in Canada do not warrant such an increase, and what, I would ask, has the minister been doing with the money? We on this side say he has been spending it recklessly and extravagantly.
When we come to the estimates which the Minister of Finance has laid before parliament for the coming year, we find that they show for next year another increase of $6,355,000 over last year But the minister is not required to spend this year all the money that he spent last year. He announces on the first page of the estimates which he has just presented to the house that he has a sum of $3,495,000 less in interest to pay this year than last; that is a large saving. We also know that there was an item in the labour estimates last year of $1,100,000 for technical education which will not be required this year. Again, last year he had to pay out $500,000 for a house for our ambassador at Washington. I hope he will not have to pay out a similar amount this year for a house in Tokyo. These three items should reduce the expenditure this year $5,095,000, and yet the minister is going to increase his expenditure by $6,355,000, or a total increase this year of between eleven and twelve million dollars over last year.
But that is not the end. Read the order paper for to-day and you will see provision is being made for loans to harbours and railways involving, as I tried to point out to the house the other day, a new expenditure of a permanent nature to the amount of $57,000,000. The truth is we have entered in this country upon a perfect carnival of extravagance. And by reason of the fact that the minister happens to have money in the treasury he is becoming grossly extravagant and is burdening the people of the country with an enormous load of taxation.
The Budget-Mr. Guthrie

Now, this is where the precise language in his budget speech fitted in so well. How careful he was when speaking on taxation to use these words:
The rate of taxation has been reduced.
Well, even that statement was not true before Friday last. But who cares about the rate of taxation? The rate does not count. The only thing that counts in this world in regard to taxes is the burden of taxation- the load which the people have to carry. If my hon. friend would read the speeches of the late William Ewart Gladstone, when he was Chancellor of the Exchequer in England, on this very point he would get some light. Gladstone pointed out very definitely that the rate of taxation means nothing; the burden of taxation means everything. And is it not true? It is the burden that the people have strapped on their backs, the burden^ they have to carry that counts. And the record of this government in regard to taxation, as disclosed in the public accounts, is one to make the people of this country think. I take again the public accounts as laid on the table of the house by the Minister of Finance, and I say to him that he has enormously increased the load of taxation borne by the people of Canada. He cannot get away from his own figures. I am going to give them in round numbers, but I will put them on Hansard as they appear in the public accounts. Again I will take the Conservative record and compare it with the minister's own record.
When you examine the consolidated revenue fund in the public accounts you must know now, if you did not know last year, for the budget speech discloses it, that eighty-seven per cent of every dollar that goes into that account is derived from taxes, and thirteen per cent comes from rents, fees and other sources. I repeat, eighty-seven per cent of every dollar which goes into the treasury is taxes. I ask the house to listen to a comparative statement upon this question. Under Conservative rule in 1918 our taxation was $260,000,000; in 1919,1312,000.000; in 1920, $349,000,000; in 1921, $434,000,000; in 1922, $381,000,000. These were war years, and we taxed practically everything we could tax. We had to have the money to carry on the war. Now I take as a comparison with the Conservative record the last five years under the administration of the present Minister of Finance. In 1925 the taxation collected amounted to $346,000,000; in 1926, $380,000,000; in 1927, $398,000,000; in 1928, $422,000,000; in
1929-this year, as announced by the minister 
in this house-$450,000,000. Of those figures which I have given you on either side, eighty-seven per cent is taken out of the pockets of the people by way of taxation. Now, mark the comparison. Five years under Conservative rule, total taxation, $1,739,000,000; five years under Liberal rule, $1,998,000,000. In other words, in the last five years this government has wrung from the people in taxes $259,000,000 more than was taken by their predecessors in the same length of time. The following is a comparative statement taken from the public accounts, page 45, of the amount of taxation collected in the fiscal years 1918-1922 and the fiscal years 19251929:

What does that mean? It means an annual increase in taxation of $51,000,000. Now, what is the burden of taxation? I got the latest figures of our population from the Bureau of Statistics, and I assume they are correct, but I think they are very optimistic. According to their estimate the population of Canada to-day is 9,658,000, which means that the taxation on every man, woman and child in Canada under this government is $5.36 more than it was under the Conservative government. This means that for a family of five the increased taxation is $26.80 per year. This enormous annual burden of taxation has been saddled upon the backs of the people by this government. These figures speak for themselves, and as they appear in the public accounts I assume they are correct. At all events, I am certain there is no member of this administration who can contradict them.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I went over those figures
before my right hon. friend came into the house. Now for a minute or two let us look at the alleged decreases in taxation. "We have decreased the rate of taxation," says the minister. The Minister of Finance has taken off the one per cent on insurance premiums. Well, I believe that yielded very little revenue anyway, but I do not know very much about it, so I will pass it over. Then he has abolished the transportation tax-one per cent on the cost of every rail-

The Budget-Mr. Guthrie
way ticket. So the man who buys a hundred dollars' worth of railway tickets in a year is going to save a dollar. But following his usual practice, the minister has taken ten per cent off the tax on parlour car and sleeping oar tickets, and has thus relieved the people in this country who are best able to pay that tax. Ninety per cent of the travelling public never enter a parlour car or a sleeper; it is the rich ten per cent of our people who do so. The rich travellers are relieved of a rather heavy tax of ten per cent, while the ordinary travelling public get one dollar of relief upon every hundred dollars of railway tickets they buy.
Again, the minister has taken three cents off telegrams and cablegrams. Now tell me, Mr. Finance minister

if I may so address him-how many telegrams the ordinary family in this country send in the course of a year. It is only in matters of domestic rejoicing and domestic calamity that they send a telegram at all; but the rich men send a lot of telegrams and cables, the big corporations send an enormous number, so do the brokers, the stock exchanges and the banks. All these will be materially relieved. And that is the very same class of people which the minister has sought to relieve in budget after budget which he has presented to this house.
When it comes down to the ordinary, everyday people of Canada, all he has to say to them is: I have taken one per cent off the sales tax. That is some relief. The sales tax last year at three per cent yielded sixty million dollars. Next year at two per cent the yield will be twenty million dollars less. But why maintain this war tax which is so burdensome upon the backs of the poorer people of the Dominion? Do the people know even yet that they have to pay two per cent on their wearing apparel, one per cent on their boots and shoes, and two per cent on practically everything that goes into the ordinary household? And yet the minister has left forty million dollars of that tax still on the people, a tax which will average at least four dollars or five dollars for every man, woman and child in the Dominion next year. I tell my hon. friend, if he would take off that forty million dollar tax burden instead of informing this house, " I have a surplus of sixty-nine million dollars," his action would be applauded throughout the country. If he had cut off forty million dollars of his surplus and forty millions of sales tax and- told the house, " I have a surplus of twenty-nine million dollars instead of sixty-nine millions," his statement would have been well received. Our taxes are ruinously excessive, they are
burdensome to the last degree, and they have been enormously increased by the present government.
Let me refer to one other remark of the Finance Minister, which he expressed in rather precise language. Indeed I thought at the time he made it he was serious. He solemnly said to the house:
This administration will refuse to support any extravagance in the spending of the taxpayers' money.
Of course we realized that it was merely a joke, whereat the Prime Minister laughed most heartily. In that respect every quarter of the house engaged in laughter, the minister himself not excepted. This bald statement as it appears in Hansard might mislead some people; they might regard it as a serious statement and not, what it was, a bit of dry Scotch humour. So that I would suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that there be permitted an interpolation in Hansard on this occasion: "Laughter, with great merriment in the house," or something of that kind, so that the people who read the minister's budget speech may not be misled. The minister cannot seriously make such a statement because he is not borne out by the facts. I charge that this has been the most wasteful and extravagant government this country has had since confederation. I am going to back up my statements with a few pointed instances.
First I would remind the house that one of the outstanding questions in the expenditure of last year or the year before related to an expenditure of $500,000 of the taxpayers' money, which was taken by this government from the taxes of the people to buy a palace in the city of Washington for the diplomatic representative of this government, instead of allowing him to rent or buy a house for himself, as should have been done. No one can justify that expenditure; it is extravagant and wasteful to the last degree, and I confront the minister with that particular expenditure as a direct challenge to the statement he made in this house last Friday that their government would tolerate no extravagance. But look at the estimates produced today. Last year the vote to maintain our Washington embassy was $60,000; to-day it stands in the estimates at $100,000-an unwarrantable and extravagant increase of $40,000. Paris, too: last year the vote for our representative stood at $75,000; now there is $5,000 more for the Paris office. No warrant for it. But in addition to that I find in the public accounts that we are maintaining another institution or agency in Paris, on which $44,000 odd was spent last year. Take Tokyo:
The Budget-Mr. Guthrie

last year in the estimates the vote was $50,000. This year, another glaring extravagance, that vote is raised to $i5,000. And there is no justification for it. And London; this government launched into a very magnificent bit of extravagant expenditure when it bought that wonderful property on Trafalgar square. There is a considerable yearly overhead to carry in respect of that property. When I was in the Meighen government the vote for the whole establishment in London was $69,000; this year the vote is $117,000 And there is absolutely no warrant for such an increase.
I have spoken of extravagance, Extravagance, I conclude, is the spending of more money than is necessary, or the spending of money unnecessarily. There is another kind of expenditure which is an absolute waste, which is the throwing away of money or the destruction of property. I charge this government not only with extravagance but I charge it also with waste. Fine properties in the city of Ottawa, worth hundreds of thousands of dollars, have been actually destroyed by the wastefulness of this government. And for what? Merely to improve the view. I am heartily in favour of improving our national capital, but I am absolutely opposed to waste in the form in which this government has permitted it to take place in this city of Ottawa.
Another thing I view as an absolute extravagance is our so-called tariff board, an absolutely useless board. This board now appears in the estimates at $120,000 a year, and I see by the public accounts that for some reason or other there was paid last year the sum of $71,000 for advisers to the tariff board. What they are doing I do not know.
I have heard it said-and I have heard it said by supporters of the government-that there is one real use for the tariff board, namely, that it acts as a buffer between the minister and some of his supporters who are always pulling his coat tail to have changes made in the fiscal policy. I say, S120,000 a year is too much to pay, even for the repose of the Minister of Finance.
Let me mention another matter which to my mind is a gross extravagance. The minister may not know about this, but he should know. Does the house realize that during the last twelve months for which the Auditor General's report contains a record this government spent-I had better be exact in this statement-for "new autos and auto repairs and renewals" the sum of $542,000? I am trying to lay these things fairly before the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance because I want them to know what is happening. I do not think they have known it 
up to this moment, but they can go to their own Auditor General's report wherein they will find some twenty-eight items, for each one of which I can give the page and the reference.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Put them on Hansard.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, I will keep them;
let them find it out. As I say, $542,000 is the amount given in the Auditor General's report for the twelve months with which it deals. I call that gross extravagance; it is a waste of the taxes of the people.
Let us pass on to something else. Look over the estimates for this year and examine the civil service vote. Why is it that year by year this government increases the number of civil servants in this country by a very large percentage? This year, I find on looking over the estimates, the increase involves 143 new civil servants. Last year it was 159, and the year before, I think, 173. What is the extra work of these departments that renders it necessary to increase the civil service of Canada at this rate? It is popularly supposed in this country that the most overmanned, most over-staffed institution in this world is the civil service of Canada. Why, in some of the departments they are falling over each other this minute; they are so numerous that they are actually hindering each other in doing proper work. And not only are we going to appoint 143 new ones, but if you look on the same page of the estimates, at the very beginning you will find $316,000 more of an annual expenditure this year for civil servants' salaries and contingencies. What these contingencies are I do not know. We vote to every department of this government a very handsome sum for contingencies-a very large amount. The government cover everything they can in their specifications in the estimates; everything they can think of, every annual and special expenditure they think necessary, is first put in. Then in addition to that we vote every year a big lump sum for contingencies; but this year they increase the vote for contingencies by $101,000. Does not the minister call that extravagance?	-
Let me give the minister another instance of what I mean by extravagance. My hon. friend can take the estimates into his room and with a blue pencil can cut them down this year twenty, yes, thirty millions, and not injure the administration of government or the public service of this country to any appreciable extent. No one would know the difference. He can take the Department of

The Budget-Mr. Guthrie
Public Works estimates alone, involving $21,-
600,000,	and blue pencil 25 per cent of that amount. Let me give him a sample of what he can do with a blue pencil. I will take the single case of the riding of North Bruce.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I thought so.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend says he
judged so; his conscience must be pricking him. North Bruce is a rural constituency projecting into the Georgian bay; it contains a delightful little town called Kincardine, one of the small towns of western Ontario, another delightful little town called Port Elgin and a couple of very small hamlets, one known as Lion's Head and another known as Tobermory. What is the record of expenditure in regard to that single riding of this Dominion? For Kincardine last year we voted $53,000 for harbour improvements and this year we are asked to vote another $50,000, of which $10,000 is a revote, making a total of $93,000. For Port Elgin this year we are asked to vote $3,000 for dredging, and my recollection is that in the public accounts for last year there was another item of $4,000. I have not. been able to verify this, although I think I have read it; the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm) will know whether or not I am right. For the little hamlet of Lion's Head last year we voted $17,800 for dredging, and this year there is another $2,600 for dredging and $4,000 for a wharf. For Tobermory, away up at the top of the Bruce peninsula, where the boys tell me there used to be some deer hunting, last year we voted $10,000 for a wharf and this year we are asked to vote another $2,000, presumably to complete the wharf. That makes a total for this one riding, containing these four small places, of. $132,000 of the taxpayers' money. Then I went to the Customs department to find the revenue from those places. They all report to Goderich; they are too small to have ports of their own, and the total revenue from all four places is only $40,000 a year.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend has the
wrong figures; we get $100,000 from Kincardine alone.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Then it must come in by the railways and not through the harbours. I took the figures from the report, which I have before me of the Customs department Then I secured the entry of vessels to these places, and I find that for the last year for which there is a report the number of vessels entering these ports was only 17, and the number of outgoing vessels 16. This may be
a very excellent way of spending public money to secure the election of political friends in various ridings but it is a very improper way to spend the taxpayers' money, and at the first opportunity the minister should blue pencil it and put a stop to this extravagant practice. My list of extravagances is by no means complete or exhaustive. I have tried to bring just a few glaring cases to the attention of the Minister of Finance and I hope he will speedily remedy the situation.
There is still another aspect of the budget to which I now wish to turn. During the whole course of the career of this government as an administration we on this side of the house charge that the government has been absolutely careless and neglectful of the interests of the ordinary people of the Dominion of Canada. When I began my remarks to-day, Mr. Speaker, I said we rejoiced over the continued prosperity in Canada, subject to certain observations I would have to make, and what I complain of is that while prosperity has been showered upon Canada for the last year or two the only evidence ot that prosperity is to be found in the large cities of Canada such as Montreal, Toronto, Hamilton, Windsor, Winnipeg, Vancouver and so on. To the ordinary smaller cities, towns and villages; in the townships and the farming districts of this country that prosperity has not yet paid a visit. I tell my hon. friend the Minister of Finance that with the exception of the few larger cities of Canada the population of this country is either stationary or retrogressing. I will take him to any of the smaller cities in the western part of Ontario, the part of the country I know best, and in each one he will find the same story according to the municipal authorities; we are making no progress and in some of these places unfortunately, we are going back. The same thing applies to the country districts in that part of the country where I reside; the villages with few exceptions are getting smaller and the number of farmers in the townships is gradually being reduced. There are more farms for sale in western Ontario to-day than there has been for the past twenty years. It is not pleasant to state these things, but these are facts which one must recognize, and this condition has been brought about largely by the indifference of this government to the people outside of the big cities or to anyone except the big interests and the big corporations, who are enjoying this so-called prosperity which has been very thinly distributed among the other classes throughout Canada.
The Budget-Mr. Guthrie

First I am going to deal with the agricultural class, and I say the condition of that class is not what it should be in any part of Canada at this moment. Before I forget it there is one matter I want to mention here in regard to the agriculturists of the west:	Evidently there is something
seriously wrong in connection with the system now in operation in regard to the grading and the sale of wheat; there is at this moment some serious difficulty in that regard in western Canada. This matter was brought to my attention last December by two gentlemen from Saskatchewan who had come to Toronto and Guelph to attend the winter fairs; they complained that they were being unfairly treated both in the grading and in the sale of their wheat. I must confess that I do not understand all the technicalities of the grain trade, but I could tell from the information given me and from the temper and earnestness of these two gentlemen that there was something radically wrong and that this government or a department of this government which is supposed to be in control of these matters was either thoroughly negligent or inefficient or both. All I can say in regard to this matter, Mr. Speaker, is that the question is so serious and affects so deeply the interests of the whole Dominion that if a grievance exists-I do not say it does, but if it does-it should be remedied before this house prorogues. If the department of government which now has control of the grading and marketing of wheat is unable to cope with the situation, let some other department take charge of this work; if the present Board of Grain Commissioners is acting improperly in any way or if the law under which they operate is improper, then let the Board of Grain Commissioners be changed or let the law be changed until the producers of this vast wealth in these western provinces are satisfied and are receiving a fair return for their capital and labour. We must recognize that the grain crop is the greatest cash asset possessed by this country, and anything which interferes with the success of the men engaged in the production of that grain is going to injure us in every corner of this Dominion of Canada.
I charge that this government has been absolutely neglectful of the interests of the farmers, and has handed them nothing but gold-bricks on several occasions. I can recall a time just prior to the general election of 1921 when the Conservative party was charged with bleeding the farmers white in regard to the duties that then existed on farm inple-ments. The farmers were told that if the 
Liberal party came into power they would reduce or abolish the tariff and that the price of farm implements would immediately come down because of the tariff reduction. Great relief was promised to the farmers in this respect, but they were merely handed a gold-brick. Notwithstanding the heavy reductions which the government made in the tariff upon farm implements, the price of farm implements has increased since 1891. I am not going over the whole list of implements, but will take just a single item which will serve as an illustration. Binders, reapers and mowers were subject to a duty of 12^ per cent when this government came into power, and they reduced it to 6 per cent. It was argued in this house that a 6 per cent reduction in the cost of a mower would be S15.96 on a $266 machine. The manufacturers were permitted to import, practically free, all the raw material that went into the manufacture of these machines, and it was said that free raw material would cause another reduction of $4 or $5 in the cost of the machine. The Finance minister of that day, Mr. Fielding, in order to appease the manufacturers, cut off the sales tax 5 per cent on farm implements, which should amount to $13.30 on a $266 machine. These total reductions amounted to $34.26, and it was openly stated that the price of the machine would be reduced to that extent. Has it been so reduced? I have obtained the prices of farm implements as of Deoember, 1921, and those in force to-day. These prices cover the McCormick-Deering, the International and the Massey-Harris machines. There will of course be a difference in the cost of freight to various points, but the prices I quote are for machines at Toronto and Montreal. In December, 1921, a six-foot binder with bundle carrier cost $235; to-day the cost has risen to $239. A six-foot binder with bundle carrier and tongue truck-in the Massey-Harris list this is called a fore-carriage, but I understand it is the same thing-cost $252 in December, 1921, while to-day the price is $254. A seven-foot binder with bundle carrier and tongue truck cost $258 in 1921, and $260 in 1928. An eight-foot binder with bundle carrier and tongue truck cost $266 in December, 1921, while to-day the price is $288.50. Notwithstanding the reductions that were made in the duty and sales tax the price is actually a little higher for binders to-day than it was in 1921. You can go through the entire price list and you will find a slight increase in prices throughout as between December, 1921, and the present time. It is not a very heavy increase, I will grant you, but I charge that

The Budget-Mr. Guthrie
the government failed in their promise to reduce the cost of farm implements, and in that respect they simply gold-bricked the farmers.
But they injured the country much more seriously than that. What did they do? They transferred a very large part of the manufacturing industry in agricultural implements from Canada to the United States. The present importations of agricultural implements are enough to shock any patriotic Canadian. Beginning with the fiscal year 1925, when the new arrangements came into force, importations of farming implements were as follows:
1925		 $ 6,494.986
1926		1 ..	13,000,000
1927		 18,000,000
1928	 29.000.000
1928	(calendar year)	 39,000,000
Every - dollar's worth of this machinery should be manufactured in the Dominion of Canada, and if that were done what a boon it would be for unemployment in this country. The agricultural implements manufactured in the shops of the United States are to a very large extent made by Canadians who have gone over there to get jobs; a tremendous number of Canadians have left Canada and are now working in the implement factories of the United States. The manufacturers of this country, while they do what they can in their own market, are forced to sell their goods to Australia, New Zealand, France and Russia, but have been able only to send about 114,000,000 worth of implements to those countries when they should be supplying their own market instead of there being importations amounting to $39,000,000 from the United States.
Perhaps the greatest gold-brick that was ever handed by a government to anyone was handed to the agriculturists of this country when the Australian treaty was passed. I understand the treaty was negotiated by the Minister of Finance himself, and it has proved to be probably the greatest direct blow that agriculture has had in this country in many years. I cannot understand why the minister does not denounce or give notice to and put an end to that treaty.at once. I have spoken in this house at a provious occasion, somewhat along the line I am taking to-day, in regard to the Australian treaty and two or three days afterwards I had an interview with a prominent paper manufacturer. He told me that I had better shut up because the paper makers were getting a mighty good thing through this treaty. That is the policy of this government; they endeavour to help those classes of the people who do not require help, such
as the newsprint men, and do not do anything for the farmers of this country. What has been the result of the operation of that treaty?
When the Minister of Finance brought the treaty before parliament not one word was uttered as to its affecting any countries other than Australia and Canada. If the minister knew otherwise he did not disclose it. I do not think the minister himself knew that he was involving Canada with New Zealand when he made this .treaty with Australia; if he had known he would have told us, and if he did not know then I do not think he should undertake to negotiate treaties with insufficient knowledge. That treaty passed the house and not one word was said about New Zealand. The house prorogued and two months afterwards we learned for the first time from the newspapers that New Zealand demanded the right to the same terms as Australia, because New Zealand was entitled to most favoured nation treatment. An order in council was passed by this government, which governs so freely by orders in council, giving to New Zealand the same right to bring her products into this country as was enjoyed by Australia. What has been the result? The Minister of Agriculture has been deluged by requests from dairymen's associations in all parts of the Dominion of Canada asking that this treaty be abrogated. Why? Because Canada is importing from New Zealand about $6,000,000 worth of butter to displace $6,000,000 worth of butter which the Canadian farmers could make in this country and could sell in the markets of this country if they were permitted to do so.
Is that fair treatment to the farming population? If the treaty was a slip on the part of the minister, why does he not say so and why does he not put an end to it? It is a terrible handicap upon the dairy industry of the Dominion to-day. Mine is not a strictly dairying constituency but there are dairymen all around it and I hear complaints on every hand. I hear the statement-and I believe it to be true-that the dairy herds in Canada are actually diminishing; that the complement of dairying is swine breeding and that the herds of swine to-day are diminishing. They are both diminishing on account of the blow which the minister gave to the agricultural industry of Canada by the Australian treaty. Then I find in the press the other side of the question, that during the last two years the dairy herds of New Zealand have increased by more than 50,000 animals and their herds of swine have increased by more than 20,000, thus demonstrating, as conclusively as possible, that this par-
The Budget-Mr. Guthrie

ticular treaty entered into by the present government has been a positive injury to the dairymen of this Dominion and a tremendous benefit to the dairymen of the sister dominion of New Zeailand.
The mistake in regard to the dairy industry was not the only one that the minister made in the negotiation of that treaty. There was one other outstanding blunder and I am going to refer to it. For the purpose of giving Australia a preference in the Canadian market in respect of a certain article known as raisins, the minister let the Australian people put one over him completely. They told him that if they got free entry they could export large quantities of raisins to Canada if Canada would place a specific duty of three cents a pound upon all importations of raisins into Canada from the rest of the world. The Australians represented that they could supply Canada with all the raisins we required and the treaty went through. We gave Australian raisins free entry into our country and we imposed a duty of three cents a pound on raisins imported from the rest of the world. What has been the result? Prior to last year we did not receive any raisins from Australia; they had not enough to supply themselves; indeed Australia was actually importing raisins for the use of her own people while we in Canada were paying into the treasury three cents on every pound of raisins that we imported from all other countries. We do not produce any raisins in this country; we get nearly all our raisins from the United States. True, we get some from Spain and other countries, but of the total importations of raisins last year amounting to some
44.000.	000 pounds, practically all came from the United States save between 3,000,000 or
4.000.	000 pounds from Australia. The duty on raisins before the treaty was only three-quarters of a cent per pound from the United States; the Minister of Finance increased the duty to three cents a pound for the benefit of Australia and the taxpayers of Canada have been contributing annually to the public treasury about $700,000, as a sort of penalty in order that Australia may at some far distant date in the future be able to supply sufficient raisins to the Canadian market. The only way in which I can describe such a result is to say that it is an outrage; it is a positive imposition upon every class of the community. Our enormous importation of raisins should be made as free as possible. As we do not produce raisins in Canada their importation does not interfere with production in this country. For many years a duty of three-quarters of a cent per pound was

levied upon raisins for revenue purposes. But now we pay a duty of three cents per pound in order to give Australia a preference which she is not able to enjoy. I say that in all these respects the government has been careless and negligent and has not safeguarded the interests of the Canadian people, and particularly the agriculturists.
The government have maintained our customs tariff at a rate which allows millions and millions of dollars' worth of agricultural produce to enter and flood the markets of Canada and to compete with similar goods produced by our own farmers. I have not made an exhaustive or complete list of these agricultural imports, but I wish the Minister of Agriculture would give me his attention while I mention some of them. Last year corn was imported into Canada to the extent of more than $13,000,000, a large part of it being used for distilling purposes and part for feeding cattle and hogs. We imported $6,745,000 worth of raw tobacco and in western Ontario we have every year a magnificent crop of Burley leaf and flue cured tobacco. Our Canadian tobacco growers are forced to compete with an importation of $6,745,000 worth of tobacco from other countries. This is most unfair to Canadian growers.
In this cattle raising country we imported $14,000,000 worth of hides, $10,000,000 of that coming from the United States. Why should we import hides? My county is a cattle county and I have heard cattle raisers discussing this question. They say that they are not getting any price for their hides. The reason will be found in the fact that we are allowing hides to come into this country so freely from the rest of the world. The Minister of Agriculture should keep his eyes and ears open at the present time. In the Argentine republic they have a great deal of cattle disease; many of the cattle have been falling on the plains. These beasts are skinned and their hides are shipped abroad. I have reason to know what I am talking about because I have had litigation in the courts and I have examined certain invoices. These hides are marked " epidemic " hides. It is a simple matter for the government to put a stop to this importation; they can do it by an increase in the tariff or by other means. Surely the farmers of this country should enjoy the market in Canada for the hides of the cattle they slaughter here, but they are not getting it now as we are importing $14,000,000 worth from the rest of the world to displace our own product in the Canadian market.

I have mentioned butter. Last year we imported 85,391,000 worth of meats. Why injure the meat trade in our own country? Why not let our own agriculturists enjoy it to the fullest extent? A few other agricultural importations are as follows:
