subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Does the hon. member include corn in that?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, but I would like someone to pick out all the agricultural items -I had not time to do it-I desire a complete list of items for another purpose which I will mention in a few minutes. It is a matter of great importance to know just what we are importing.
An industry of very great importance in this country is the fruit industry which is established in Nova Scotia on a wonderful scale, in New Brunswick, on the southern shores of the river St. Lawrence where they produce Fameuse apples in abundance and throughout Ontario in general but especially in the Niagara peninsula between Niagara and Windsor, and also throughout British Columbia. Why allow this immense importation of foreign fruit practically to put out of business many of our fruit growers? We must admit that the United States has in the matter of climate an advantage which we cannot overcome.	United States fruit comes on the
market two or three weeks before ours is ready. There is a public appetite for new fruit when it first comes to market, and people are willing to pay high prices for this early fruit, but when that initial appetite is satiated our own crop is about ready and the market is glutted with fruit, and in far too many cases our own fruit is not plucked and gathered at all. Last August, between Toronto and Hamilton, I saw field after field of beautiful melons. "Why don't you pick your melons and send them to market?" I asked, and the reply was "They won't pay for the labour. They will not give me anything for them.
The Budget-Mr. Guthrie
These people in Toronto," he said, "are fed up with this American stuff, and they do not want our melons at all." It is the same in every line. Look at the fruit importations into Canada. According to the trade returns, we imported last year-I shall give only round
figures:
Apples	 $1,124,000
And yet in this country we grow the finest apples in the world:
Grapes	 $1,189,000
Melons	 498,000
Peaches	 663,000
Pears	 928,000
Plums	 544,000
Strawberries	   832,000
Other fruits, including cherries. 408,000
We imported all this fruit from the United States a few weeks in advance of the ripening of our own Canadian crops, thereby displacing the Canadian fruit grower in his own market, and in far too many cases making his occupation unproductive altogether.
It is the same with vegetables. Up around Windsor we grow a tremendous quantity of onions. Last year there was a good crop. -Last year we imported $548,000 worth of onions. Take new potatoes, not the kind we sell as winter potatoes; we imported of new potatoes $799,000 worth. We imported tomatoes to the amount of $1,550,000. These are very largely of the hothouse variety, and our people around Windsor are engaged in that very class of production. We imported other vegetables to the amount of $3,371,000. Total vegetable importations amounted to $8,475,000, and of these, $6,496,000 were from the United States. These latter figures include canned and dried vegetables.
The indifference of the government in regard to the claims of the agriculturists, because these people all are agriculturists, was never better exemplified, I think, than by an answer made by the Prime Minister in this house to a question asked by my hon. friend from South Essex (Mr. Gott) on the orders of the day on Tuesday last. Evidently the hon. member for East Essex (Mr. Odette) had circulated some statement up around Windsor to the effect that the government was going to take action this session and put a duty on fruits and vegetables. That rumor got into the Windsor press, and the vegetable growers, who are a very important pan ot that community, sent to Ottawa to ascertain whether there was any truth in this rumor. When the question was asked in this House of Commons by my hon. friend from South Essex, my right hon. friend the Prime Minister, as, of course, he has a right to do, gave no information

The Budget-Mr. Guthrie

whatever upon this question which at the present moment is of very vital concern to the vegetable growers in the county of Essex. These growers are now preparing for the coming season. Last season most of them lost money. They expected last year that a dumping clause duty would be put into effect, but it was not, and they were expecting some relief this year from the government particularly in view of the statement of the hon. member for East Essex. The question was asked in this house in the most natural and proper way, "Would the government do anything?" But the Prime Minister gave absolutely no information, and he did not even say that he would give any information on the matter at a later date, although these men are waiting from day to day to get their seeds and plants in, and their hothouses going to start the season's operations. If they are not going to get any relief this year, let them know it, and then they will go into some other line, because there is no use continuing in their present line under the conditions that prevailed in that part of the country last season.
I now wish to deal for a few minutes with the industrial workers of Canada, with that class of men who are known as wage-earners, who form a large and important class in this country and who earn their living by their daily wage. I charge again that throughout its whole course of seven or eight years this government has absolutely neglected to safeguard the interests of the wage-earners, or to protect their rights in any single instance. I know that my hon. friend the Minister of Finance made a few bland announcements the other day, but he forgot to say anything about the high cost of living. He remembers, just as I do, the election of 1921, when the charge was levelled against the government then in power that the cost of living had risen in Canada to such a point that people could no longer endure it, and I have no doubt that that statement changed a good many votes on that occasion. Does my hon. friend know that the cost of living is just a little higher in Canada to-day than it was in 1921? If he does not, he had better read the journal issued by the Labour department of this government, and bearing the official stamp of the Labour department, and he will find that it shows that the cost of living is a trifle higher to-day than it was when this government took office. He will find likewise that the family budget to-day-I assume that these figures are correct, because the Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan) is responsible for them-the family budget of nineteen necessary articles, including fuel and 
light, was in January, 1922, $21.52 per family, and to-day it is $21.55 per family; that is, the cost of living is a trifle higher to-day in Canada than in those awful days when it was freely charged by Liberals that the former Conservative government was practically starving the people to death.
The minister also states in his budget speech that employment has been well maintained. Why, sir, there is just as much unemployment in Canada to-day as there was the day this government came into power.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What is your employment index?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am going to give it
to the house in a moment. There has been little or no change in the intervening years, and what change there has been, according to the returns, has been against this government, because employment is a little lower to-day than it was when this government came into power. If anyone wants evidence of unemployment in Canada, all he has to do is go to Toronto, Montreal or Winnipeg, or read the bulletin that was issued by the civic authorities in Toronto last month showing that eight thousand men were willing to work and could not find jobs. If you are not satisfied with this statement, look at page 55 of the estimates for the coming year, and you will see there a vote of a quarter of a million dollars proposed by this government to help people who are unemployed. What better evidence do you want?
My hon. friend from North Battleford (Mr. McIntosh) asked for the index figure. I am not going to give the figures for the years 1920 or 1921, the demobilization years, when we were bringing back to Canada and demobilizing and bringing home 420.000 troops, as well as 240,000 troops in Canada, and when the employment figures were not normal. But for the month of December. 1922, according to the table furnished by the Department of Labour, the percentage of unemployment was 6-4. Taking the same month, December, last year, unemployment had increased in the interval to 6-6. So unemployment has not vanished. I only refer to unemployment at all to show that this wonderful prosperity that we hear about has not been well distributed among the people of this country. The working class, the wage earners of Canada, have not had their chance to share in it.
Let me mention one further matter. This unemployment situation in Canada could be cured by the government almost by a stroke of the pen. My good friend the Minister of Finance could cure it this session. He could

The Budget-Mr. Guthrie
cause employment in this country to be abundant and at good wages. He could stop the exodus of our people to the United States. This exodus has not stopped yet, for every United States consular agent in Canada still has a waiting list of Canadians anxious to go to that country. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance could settle the difficulties of his colleague the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Forke); he could settle the immigration problem in this country by creating employment, and he could do that by the application of a proper fiscal policy for this Dominion. We imported last year $350,000,000 of goods- and this is only an abbreviated list-and these were goods that we make in this country. The action of the Minister of Finance and the government has not been to assist labour. Take the removal of the duty on worsted yarns last year. I do not know whose advice the Minister of Finance was taking or what prompted him to remove this duty, although I have always believed that it was the Bradford board of trade in England, which certainly was in communication with the minister and his tariff board; but last year, the minister, by a stroke of the pen, wiped out the worsted yarn business in this country. The great big worsted spinning mill at Hespeler, where hundreds of men were employed, is now closed. The industry in Guelph is also stopped; in Guelph, worsted spinning only formed part of a larger woollen industry but the spinning of worsted yarns has practically ceased. All the worsted yarns used in Canada are now brought from Bradford, Yorkshire. The men in Canada are out of work, their employment has been transferred from Canada to Great Britain, and the price of worsted yam and worsted clothing is just the same to-day as it was last year. That I give only as a sample. Look at the imports of woollens. This government tinkered with the woollen tariff when they first came into power. What has been the result? Our woollen imports increased to thirty-three million dollars last year. Practically all of these goods we could have produced here. Look at the employment that would be given our people. There is no question about it, Mr. Speaker, that-with half a dozen strokes of the pen the Minister of Finance could settle this question of unemployment, could make the factories of this country boom, could keep young Canadians in Canada, and could create an active cash market for all the products of the Canadian farm.
But we have been pursuing a policy of practical min not only in this but in many other respects. I do not charge this government particularly in regard to the export of raw 78594-48$
material, because I think the same system has prevailed for many years; but I do say that this question of the export of our raw materials to the United States has been brought to the attention of this government in a very definite shape upon many occasions during recent years, but they simply allow that exportation of raw materials to go on. They permit those valuable natural resources, those raw materials of the Dominion, to go into the United States at the rate of millions of dollars' worth every year. The factories of the United States are kept busy, the citizens of the United States get wages, and the people of the United States get the tremendous profit between the price of the raw material and the manufactured article which we buy back again from the United States. It is a false policy, it is a suicidal policy. Rapidly it is denuding our forests and exhausting our mines, and the minister should give serious consideration to the question.
My next reference brings up a matter which I know must be in the minds of most of our people. On Monday last when the President of the United States delivered his inaugural speech at Washington he announced to his countrymen and to the world that he had summoned a special meeting of congress particularly to consider the fiscal policy of the United States in regard to agricultural productions. In a good many quarters of course that announcement was not entirely unexpected. The policy of the Republican party in the United States during the late fall elections was a policy of greater protection for the agriculturists. I realize full well, Mr. Speaker, that while we have the right to discuss the fiscal policy of any other country in the world, it is not really a matter of our own business, and we must recognize the right of the United States to adopt such a fiscal policy as it deems fit without interference from us or from any other nation. For at least three-quarters of a century the fiscal policy of the United States has been one of protection, or, as I would say, of very high protection in many respects. Consistently they have maintained that principle, and as a result they find themselves to-day not only the richest, but the greatest commercial nation in the world, and the nation having the largest population in the world. Tremendous success has attended their efforts and their policy. For myself, I see no real cause for overanxiety in Canada in regard to any action which may be taken by congress upon the fiscal policy of the United States. I believe that we are in so strong and favoured a position in this Dominion that nothing more than

The Budget-Mr. Guthrie
temporary embarrassment or temporary inconvenience could result, no matter what attitude the United States government and congress may assume. But I base that statement wholly upon this condition, that we enjoy in this Dominion a government with sufficient resolution and sufficient courage to meet any situation which may arise. If we have not such a government, then I do see some real ground for anxiety as to what may face us in the immediate or more remote future.
When the Minister of Finance made his budget speech he gave the house a clear statement of the total trade of Canada based on exports and imports. Let me repeat it. I am taking the calendar year ending on December 31 last. There is a good deal of difficulty sometimes in adjusting the figures between the calendar and the fiscal year. These figures are for the calendar year ending December 31 last:
Total Trade, Domestic and Foreign
Exports	$1,374,130,000
Imports	 1,222,318,000
Total	$2,596,448,000
And the minister announced, amid great applause and approval by his supporters, that he had a favourable balance of trade of $154,000,000. That, I grant, is a substantial favourable balance. As I say, this statement was well received by his followers; they applauded to a very marked degree; they approved of the announcement by a marked demonstration.
Now let us return to our trade figures with the United States. It may be a matter of surprise to some that more than one-half of our total foreign trade is done with the United States. Last year our trade figures with the United States give us a total in exports and imports of $1,318,282,000. We imported $825,741,000, and we exported $492,-
541,000.	In other words, our imports were $333,000,000 more than our exports; therefore our trade with the United States resulted in an unfavourable balance of that amount. Now, if a favourable balance of trade is a good thing for a nation-and the minister's announcement was heartily applauded on the other side of the house-what do these hon. gentlemen say of our trade with the United States when there results such an enormous unfavourable balance? Will hon. gentlemen opposite condemn that unfavourable balance of trade? They applauded the favourable balance of trade with the world as an excellent thing. Will they condemn our unfavourable balance of trade with the United States as an injurious thing?

I submit, Mr. Speaker, that there is something seriously wrong in regard to the trade of this country with the United States. I believe I know what is wrong. I believe that we are buying too much from the United States year in and year out and are selling too little. Every year our purchases are increasing, and we are not selling enough to our neighbours, because they will only buy from us raw materials and a limited amount of farm products. At the end of the fiscal year our operations resulted, as I have shown, in an adverse balance of trade of S333,000,000. That balance has to be settled. We have to pay it either in gold or in goods. It cannot go on forever; it must be paid, and the money or the goods to pay it will have to come from this country.
Now it is worth while considering in a little more detail some of the trade figures as between Canada and the United States. What do we sell them? How shall we be affected by a change in the fiscal policy of the United States in regard to agricultural products? In our trade figures, as furnished by the Department of Trade and Commerce, it is just a little difficult at all times to find what are really farm products and what are not; our trade returns include in the figures a good many articles which are not strictly farm products. Let me give a rough analysis of some of these figures. I find that in agricultural and vegetable products we sell to the United States, according to our trade returns, $56,000,000 in round figures. That I grant is a large amount. But I find that included in that figure are ales, wines, beers, whiskies and rubber, amounting to $24,500,000-commodities that are not farm products in our view of the matter. These should be deducted from the $56,000,000, leaving a total of exports to that country, in agricultural and vegetable products, of some $31,550,000. When you come to the next classification, you find some further trouble-animals and animal products. This heading covers much more than farm products. Our trade returns show that we sent to the United States last year, in animals and animal products, $92,000,000 worth of exports. But when you come to analyse the items you find included in the total, fish, $13,000,000; furs, $14,000,000; leather, $8,000,000; oils and greases, $1,399,000, or a total of some $39,000,000 of goods which we do not consider strictly farm products. This amount should be deducted from the $92,000,000, and would leave a balance, under animals and animal products, of $42,385,000, or a total of agricultural products, properly so described, shipped to the United States, of $73,935,000.

The Budget-Mr. Guthrie
I think we can fairly cut that figure down by another $10,000,000. We send the United States about $10,000,000 worth of raw hides and we buy from them $10,000,000 of raw hides. That item forms merely a cross entry. If our neighbors see fit to stop our hides from going to the United States we will use our own hides in our own country instead of importing them, and that will settle that point. So that we find actually that we sell them, in agricultural or farm products, as we understand the term, only $63,000,000 a year. We import from the world in farm products something between $50,000,000 and $60,000,000 a year.

speechtext:
Will my hon. friend
specify the figures as he did in the other

I put them on Hansard

speechtext: But specified imports.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I gave the agricultural
imports, starting with corn. I furnished a list of only some of them. My list was not exhaustive, and it runs to over $50,000,000, probably $60,000,000, of farm products which we are bringing into Canada from other countries to compete with the products of our own farmers. That is what we are bringing in, while we are sending out to the United States if you exclude hides, only about $63,000,000 or less than ten per cent of our agricultural exports.
Would it not be a simple matter under these circumstances, to obviate any difficulty that might arise in connection with the tariff of the United States on farm products, if we produced in this country and sold to our own people those goods which we now sell to the United States, stopping the importation into Canada of those products which we are now bringing from other countries to compete with the products of our own farmers. To accomplish that, all we need is a government with some courage; all we need is a government with some resolution; all we need is a government that has at heart the real interests of the people, of the farmers of Canada. With such a government no permanent difficulty can ever arise.
Now I can see that any disarrangement of our present trade with the United States might for the time being cause considerable inconvenience, and some loss. I realize quite well that in many respects the United States market is the most convenient, the most expedient market which we have; in many respects it is the very best market in which to sell many of our farm products.
But if the tariff of that country is raised so high that we cannot enjoy that market, then we shall have to shape ourselves accordingly by enabling our own farmers to enjoy the Canadian market to the fullest extent and at the same time seek other markets throughout the world. In order to do this, however, we shall need to have a fair application of the principle of protection in our customs tariff. And unless we adopt that principle, if the United States government sees fit to raise its tariff against our farm products, great difficulty will probably ensue in connection with the marketing of $63,000,000 of our farm products in the future.
I can conceive a situation which would seriously affect the shipment of our cattle to the United States. Last year we shipped to the United States $17,745,000 under this head. An adverse tariff might cause inconvenience and some loss for the time being in this regard. Our grain shipments were about $10,000,000-nothing like what I imagined they would be. In vegetables our whole shipment consists practically of about $5,000,000 in potatoes and, in turnips, about $700,000 or $800,000. We do send a large number of seeds to the United States; last year we sold them about $6,000,000 worth. Surely we can find another market for these seeds. In raw furs we sent them $14,000,000; hides, $11,000,000- and we bought back $10,000,000; meats, $11,288,000. This is a big item and one in respect to which there might be some temporary embarrassment and inconvenience. In milk and milk products the figure is
S10,000,000, or nearly $11,000,000, and in this connection too the situation might be serious for the time being; while in hay the figure is about $1,000,000 or $1,200,000, and in bran and shorts about $2,000,000 to $2,500,000. These, so far as I can see, are the only articles with respect to which we could possibly be inconvenienced or for a time be seriously affected. So far as I can see, any difficulty that may possibly arise in the future can be completely overcome by action on the part of this government and of this parliament. We have nothing to fear in Canada in this respect, though I grant that we are going to reach at last a situation-if things develop as I anticipate they will-in which we must introduce into the tariff of this country, to protect our own people, that element of protection which the Canadian tariff does not now afford.
I can imagine that it will not be the easiest thing for my right hon. friend the Prime Minister, surrounded as he is by such out and out free traders as the Minister ol
75S
The Budget-Mr. Guthrie

Agriculture, the Minister of Railways, the Minister of the Interior, who would ring the death knell of protection in the House of Commons, and the Minister of Immigration. I can understand that my right hon. friend will have difficulty. But I fancy that these four ministers will be found amenable to reason. I believe that in a few months' time we shall find that they have become converts to the doctrines which have been advocated from this side of the house for a long time and which they have denounced. And I can tell you that the completeness and the suddenness of their conversion will rival that famous conversion that took place many centuries ago on the road to Damascus. But what about that peculiar type of free traders-Liberal free traders-whom we find scattered about in all the provinces of Canada? What will these Grit free traders do-these loud-voiced individuals who give us no peace, these worshippers at the shrine of Adam Smith, these men who still dwell in the political atmosphere of two centuries ago? I think I can make a prediction in that regard. I believe the word of command will go to them to "right about face", and they will obey that command with alacrity. Oh, the scales will fall from the eyes of these hard-shelled, thick-skinned free traders who are to be found scattered throughout this Dominion of Canada. I predict that by next year it will be found that they have shed their free trade skins and taken on new ones, and they will remind one of nothing so much as the snakes coming out of the stone piles in the spring. A radical change in our fiscal policy will soon be necessary; the government must face this situation. They can do it; we know what we can do in this country; we have everything at our disposal. Do not let us have stage fright and do not let us feel any over-anxiety in regard to the matter. The matter rests entirely in our own hands. All can be put right, and if this government does not put it right another government will take its place in the very near future.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I have transgressed for a long time on the patience of the house. For the reasons I have given, because this government has been absolutely neglectful of the interests of at least seventy-five per cent of the people of this country, neglectful of the interests of the agriculturists and of those engaged in industrial employment; because the government has failed in every way to safeguard and protect them, I beg to move the following amendment, seconded by the hon. member for Argenteuil (Sir George Perley):

That all the words after the word "that" be stricken out and the following substituted therefor:
This house regrets that the financial proposals of the government make no provision for reasonably safeguarding and protecting the interests of those "engaged in agricultural pursuits or in industrial" employment in Canada.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while listening to the very comprehensive and forceful criticism presented by the acting leader of the opposition (Mr. Guthrie) I must say that for a considerable time I was inspired with some fear; I was afraid he would not leave one single charge for me to make against the government. Seeing that he covered the ground so thoroughly I hoped he might have continued until six o'clock in order to give me an opportunity of finding something with which he had not dealt. Fortunately, however, there were one or two points which he failed to cover.
I think I might characterize the budget now before the house as a comfortable budget. It suggests to the mind a fairly well-fed ruminating animal which, having eaten all the grass it wanted, lies down to chew its cud on the sunny side of a knoll quite unconscious of the fact that the frost of the preceding night had practically destroyed the crop and might prejudice its existence when winter comes. All finance ministers in their budget presentation strive to strike a political key-note throughout the country. Sometimes, of course, that key-note is drowned out by the carillon of debts and deficits, and sometimes the announced surpluses and balances jangle strangely out of tune. From a comparative study of budgets I have noticed that when a minister has to deal with deficits he never fails to point out very clearly that such defiicits are not at all due to any mismanagement on his part, to any lack of business acumen or any failure of government policy, but when he has the pleasure of announcing a surplus he never fails to show that such surplus was accounted for by the most excellent policy of his administration. That, of course, is what we might call the human and political element of the budget.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hurrah.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I hope time will be taken
off for the interruptions now taking place. Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, you might send someone to the lobby to tell those gentlemen who are cheering that as yet I have not finished speaking.
When the loud cheering began, Mr. Speaker, I was pointing out that when a minister announces a surplus in his budget he is very anxious to claim that it is due to a certain

The Budget-Mr. Irvine
policy of his administration, but we have discovered that a true explanation of prosperity in our national life must be sought in economic factors with which governments have very little to do. As a financial statement the budget now before parliament does not require a very great deal of criticism or opposition, indeed, I would congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) and his staff upon being able to add correctly. I find that all the millions are added properly and all the subtractions correctly carried out; we find that we have an estimated expenditure of $385,160000, that we have a total estimated revenue of $454,942,000, and when we subtract the smaller figure we have a surplus of $69,782,000.
I might also congratulate the minister upon the splendid way in which he presented his budget to the house. I should like to impress upon him that I have a very high opinion indeed of his ministerial ability, and in addition to those lower qualities which are required of financiers and accountants generally the minister possesses others of more value. For instance, he is genuinely human, and he possesses a vein of humour so rich and deep that it takes a real Scot to sound it. Listen to this priceless gem which fell from his lips just after they had let fall the mighty millions resulting from his own tariff policy. He said:
The policy of this administration is not a high tariff policy; it is a low tariff policy. Its policy is to encourage production at home and the marketing of our excess of production abroad.
It is not every minister who has the genius to inject humour into the millions of surpluses, debts and so on. Again, the minister said:
In the first ten months of the fiscal year the Department of Rational Revenue reports total exports amounted to $1,187,400,000, which, when the total imports of $1,033,300,000 are subtracted, leaves a favourable trade balance of $154,100,000 for the ten months' period.
If statements like these emanated from an uninformed source, and were regarded by those who uttered them as being indicative of the economic position of the people of Canada, we would regard them with the contempt they truly merited; but, coming as they do from a well informed source, they can be appreciated only when seen in the humorous setting in which they appear. Everyone knows that the budget under the party system of government, with which we are cursed at the present time, means more than a mere addition and subtraction of millions of dollars. It contains the entire plot of a play. The stage is set, and after due advertising the minister appears in the dual capacity of hero and villian, depending on which side of the house hon. gentlemen contemplating
him happen to be sitting. The population both in and out of parliament are waiting breathlessly; the moment is melodramatic it is true, but eventually the minister enters and announces a surplus. Sometimes the artistry of this particular show is drowned in the swelling flood of millions, and also encompassed with political humbug. The time has come, Mr. Speaker, to lodge an emphatic objection to the technique of party government, of which this and other budgets are expressions. What have hon. members of the house had to do with the budget now before them? The deliberative functions of parliament have been practically usurped by the party system. In the hodge-podge of figures, fiscal policy, debts, international trade and surpluses with which the mind is suddenly deluged, members have no part to play whatever. If we had, I venture to say that there are many things not in this budget which would be in it, and there are some things in it which would not be in it. But ours not to reason why, ours but to vote the pie for the noble six hundred. Let me illustrate the position of the private members of this house. I am sure the Minister of Finance, genial as he is, will forgive me for setting him in a particular scene which will illustrate my point. I am going to make him a chef in a first-class cafe, and I am going to give him the rest of the cabinet as his waiters. The members of parliament, the representatives of the people, of course, will be the patrons of this cafe.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Who gets the tips?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
WTe all come in for our
meal at the usual hour, and the Prime Minister, all dressed up in his proper habiliments for the occasion, presents us with the menu. We look it over and find that there are many things on the menu we do not like. There are some things we might like but we could not possibly accommodate all that is on the menu. However, we are told by the chef and the waiter that no selection is to be permitted; that we have to swallow it all from the consomme of tariff reduction to the surplus pie and the national debt pudding with the income tax sauce. We cannot make any selection from the menu; the dictum of the institution is that we must take it all or leave it. We have some dieticians who think that perhaps a better bill of fare could be arranged. We have others who are willing to close their eyes and open their mouths and take whatever comes, but those of us who desire the right to deliberate upon matters which come before this house regard
The Budget-Mr. Irvine

the budget and the manner of its preparation as being the very opposite of true representative government, and absolutely void of the democratic principle which is supposed to inhere in this parliament. We neither deliberate nor create any detail of this budget. We are asked to give it a blanket endorsation or a blanket condemnation. Let me suppose for a moment, Mr. Speaker, that what I am saying is as wise as I think it is.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Impossible.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I knew the hon. member would be able to observe the obvious. Supposing for the sake of argument that it is as wise as I think it is. I am allowed to say it, but that is all. This parliament has perfect freedom in so far as speech is concerned, but when it comes to actually doing something we have the limits of the robot. I think the time has come when every member of parliament, who ought to be in the position of truly representing his constituents, should expose this sophistry of representative government, expose the sophistry of the supremacy of parliament, and indicate to the people the truth of the matter

the supremacy of cabinets in our system of government. Our cabinets have the power to give away our water sites. They tell us we can ratify their actions, or if we do not we defeat the government. They give away other things equally as valuable as the water-powers. They sign treaties that may have a far-reaching effect upon the peace of the world, and then come and ask us to ratify them. They bring down the budget, which has important economic and political implications, and we are not permitted to change one jot or tittle within the entire compass of that budget. All we can do is to take or leave it; take all or none. The Minister of Finance virtually comes to this parliament and says, "There is the budget, fix it if you dare." If we did fix it, according to the powers which we are supposed to have but cannot exercise, then he would dissolve parliament and we would have to assume the responsibility of having plunged the country into an election. This massive club of dissolution is always held over the heads of parliamentarians. I wonder if the members of the house could not swing the club of dissolution the other way once in a while. I wonder if the ministers are so immune to election fears that they would not pay any attention to that. I would like to psycho-analyse the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) and find out if he would not yield a point or two were that club swung over his head, and I am sure there are others who might be led to

consider following the same course. If hon. members asserted themselves we could force parliament from beneath the heel of cabinet domination. This is a phase of parliament which is most disgusting to the Canadian people, which is most discouraging to hon. members who have any intelligence; it deprives them of that nominal responsibility which they are supposed to have towards those whom they represent.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker looking at the
budget from another angle, I Should like to point out that it implies more than a mere financial statement. Under our system of government the budget reflects national policy and sometimes unfortunately it reveals the extent of statesmanship possessed by those on the treasury benches. It is a looking glass which reflects not only the ruddy face of the genial Minister of Finance but also the background of policy. I notice that standing out very prominently in the background of policy is the national debt. It stands out like a sore thumb that has received first aid from the minister. Of course there is a political setting given to this. The party which was in power prior to the present administration is inferentially shown as the debt creating party and the government of to-day is of course held up as the debt paying party. But when we come to examine into the details of the budget we discover who has been doing the paying and we have to admit that the masses of the people, especially the agricultural class, have been charged a great deal more in taxation than any other class for the surplus out of which a certain amount of the debt was paid last year. We find also that the people who ought to be able to pay more than anybody else have been taxed less.
But let me turn to the larger question of debt payment. Let me presume to suggest to the minister that payment of debt is an operation which requires a great deal of skill and caution in its performance. No doubt he is aware that there are times when debts should not be paid even if the government were in a position to pay them. There are times when to pay debts would very materially interfere with the business and industrial success of the country. If, for instance, the minister, because he happens to have a few millions in the treasury, rushes off to pay

The Budget-Mr. Irvine
debts at a time when we are passing through industrial depression, it is altogether unlikely that such amounts of money as he paid would find opportunity for reinvestment and the result would be that, through removing from circulation the amount of the debt he paid h-e would force us into further depression. So there is a real problem there which I suggest for his consideration.
But I want the minister's attention on one point and I should like to emphasize it. It is that debts cannot be paid in the popular sense of the word "paid". I do not mean they cannot be paid because the amounts are so great that they are beyond our assets. That is not exactly true, although they are certainly great enough. I mean to say that they cannot be paid because our financial system is a debt creating system. Our financial system lives on debt, lives by debt, lives for debt and without debt it cannot live. If our debts could be paid in the sense in which most people accept the idea of payment, our system would collapse. It is the very nature of the financial system of which the minister is at the head to pyramid debts, debts built on debts built on debts, until the entire system is threatening to topple over, and it is more than the average individual can do to interfere in any way with that pyramiding. It requires a fundamental alteration of policy and one which the minister alone is in position to introduce.
The debt of Canada as of all other countries to-day is increasing by the principle of geometrical progression and it cannot be affected as long as the present system is in vogue. What does the minister mean when he tells us that he has paid so many millions of debt ? He simply means that he has transferred a public to a private debt. Let me illustrate that in this way. Supposing he finds himself next year with a surplus of $100,000,000 which he has collected through over-taxation of the poor people of Canada; he proceeds to the Bank of Montreal, takes up $100,000,000 worth of bonds and makes a bonfire of them. What happens after that? That amount of $100,000,000 will immediately become somebody else's debt. The banks cannot afford to pay, for instance, 31 per cent on $100,000,000 if they don't lend it out. As soon as the bank does lend that $100,000,000 it becomes somebody else's debt. Individuals whose bonds are taken up may make their own investment so that in any case, the amount paid on national debt must become private debts except it were withdrawn from circulation. So to pay debt is merely a transference of a national debt to a private debt, but with this
difference, that on the national debt we are paying presumably about 5 per cent whereas on the private debt we are paying probably 8 per cent and that charge comes back to the consuming public in terms of prices, whereas the minister charges us the interest in terms of taxation. Therefore I hope the minister will be more careful when he is, in a human way of course, making political capital out of the fact that he has succeeded in reducing our debt in the last few years by a few million dollars.
This brings me to the guileless allusion of the minister to the Canadian dollar. He clothes that abstract instrument with personality, perches it on the boundary line with a flag in its hand, and causes it to say: "I, the Canadian dollar, can now look the American dollar square in the eye without blushing," and then he expects us to applaud for the great contribution which he has made in bringing about what he regards as that very satisfactory state of affairs. Rejoice with me, he says, because our dollar can now, without blushing, look the American dollar in the face. Mr. Speaker, that simply means nothing. Let me say plainly to the ,Minister of Finance that his inability or his disinclination to control the dollar value after the war was the means of doubling our national debt. Germany, we are told, and we believe, lost the war, and Canada won the war, but I discover that the per capita debt of Germany in 1926, was $8.76, while the per capita debt of Canada, which won the war, was, in 1927, $246.64. Canada's high per capita debt came about through the bankers' manipulation of credit, which the minister did not hinder, as he might have done. Everybody knows now that that manipulation was a bad thing. Even Lord Beaverbrook has been very outspoken on this point very recently. He says:
The Bank of England's policy in adopting the gold standard was ill-considered and ill-advised.
He goes on to say that the bankers dictated the industrial policy of the country. He continues:
We have had a bankers' policy all along, directed along the lines of favouring the general financial situation without regard to the industrial situation.
This has resulted in a per capita debt in Great Britain, which won the war, of $817.60, while Germany, which lost the war, has a per capita debt of $8.76.
Someone may suggest, do I advocate doing what Germany did? I would say in reply that what Germany did was a great deal more advisable than what Canada did, although it
;62
The Budget-Mr. Irvine

is not the course that I myself would recommend. The responsibility, I would say, was upon the Minister of Finance to have stabilized the value of the Canadian dollar on a war basis so that the dollar with which he now pays the debt would have had precisely the same value as the dollar with which the debt was contracted. But instead of doing that, the minister permitted the dollar to drop from its inflation value to its present deflation value, which practically doubled the Canadian war debt, plus five per cent; so that, due to the inactivity of the minister during the first few years that he was in office, he has placed a greater debt on the shoulders of the Canadian people than he will ever live to see removed, no matter how high he taxes the people. If the minister will ponder that problem, he will find that as the financial controller of Canada he has burdened the Canadian people with debt, and if he is satisfied that I am right in that, I hope that next year he will be apologetic and not try to make political capital out of what may be the fact, that he has reduced the debt yearly by an average of 137,000,000.
In his budget speech the minister deals in a very careless way with foreign trade and trade balances. He announced a favourable trade balance-mark the word "favourable"-of $154,000,000. This gives the impression that that $154,000,000 of a trade balance is in some strange way favourable to Canada, and that idea will no doubt be the basis of the Liberal party's propaganda in the press for the next few months. If there is a balance, it has been erroneously named a favourable balance. Trade, of course, is a fair exchange of goods, and if what the minister reports is true, then Canada has given away $154,000,000 for which she has received nothing. Otherwise, international trade cannot be a fair and equitable exchange of goods. On what basis does the minister do trade with foreign countries if it is not on an equitable basis? By what strange manipulation is he able to build up a favourable balance of trade anywhere in the world? The thing is utterly preposterous. It is a schoolboy's idea of international trade. Surely, if we have $154,000.000 worth of foreign trade more than we can handle, the minister does not need to look to other countries for greater markets than we now possess.
Let us look at it another way. I challenge the minister and his entire staff to come within two hundred million dollars of guessing the correct balance of trade between Canada and other countries of the world, because the technique of accountancy in this particular
(Mr. Irvine.]
department of political economy has not yet been thoroughly established, and there cannot be anything which is much more than a guess at the balance; there must be a wide margin permitted for error. But we do know that when all invisibles are accounted for, such as tourist trade, interest on loans, freight payments, as well as capital transactions, then international trade must balance, or else the minister has been giving away our goods and been getting nothing for them in return. Which is the situation? Will the minister tell us which of the two it is? Has he been negotiating with other countries to take our goods for nothing, or has he wrongly reported a trade balance of $154,000,000? This seems to amuse the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) very much. I do not know whether he is amused at the political economy of his colleague the Minister of Finance, or whether he is amused at the ease with which the minister's argument can be exploded.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am amused at your
political economy.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am delighted that the
minister has grasped it to the extent of being amused by it. Perhaps further consideration may change his amusement to something of understanding. Let me give an example to the hon. gentleman. In 1020, it was reported that we had an unfavourable balance of $268,000,000; in 1921, an unfavourable balance of $137,000,000, and in 1922, an unfavourable balance of $68,000,000. These adverse balances were made up of funds advanced to Great Britain during the war, and which were being repaid. In 1920, we received on that account $104,000,000; in 1921, $128,000,000, and in 1922, $84,000,000 thus the unfavourable balance vanished.
Our favourable balance means that Canada has increased her capital investments abroad. I want to draw the attention of the house to this fact, that during the war there was one and one-quarter billions of new money circulated in Canada, and corralled by those who had .privileges, and that really marks the extent of our national debt. Now those people are looking for outlets for the reinvestment of their money, and if they do not find what they want in Canada-they are not very patriotic-they go where they can find suitable opportunities for investment.
Let me also point out to the minister that the balance of trade is to a considerable extent made up of investments by insurance companies in foreign securities abroad. The minister should take a hand in controlling that situation, and endeavour to keep that

The Budget-Mr. Irvine
money in. Canada, to finance the government of this country and look after the purchasing power of our own people. Let me ask the minister to tell us, the next time he brings down a budget, how much of the balance of trade goes to .paying interest on borrowings abroad, borrowings which ought to have been made in Canada through the use of the Finance Act and the treasury board.
Passing from that, I think this budget will be regarded in western Canada as the "hame-strap budget". The Minister of Finance says that he has not reduced the tariff because the tariff board has not had time to make sufficient investigation in the three years it has been sitting. But I would point out to the members of the house that the tariff board has managed in that time to discover one kind of hame-strap on which the tariff ought to be reduced. However, it is too late now for that, because most of the farmers are using tractors and tractors do not require hame-etraps. Furthermore, the promised tariff reductions have not been satisfactorily met. True, there have been small reductions in the sales tax, but the greatest, tax of all, the tariff tax which falls on the common people generally, has not been touched, and to that extent we must hold the government responsible for their failure to redeem their promises.
As to how their fiscal policy compares with the announced policy upon which the Liberal party came into power, let me quote one section from the resolution passed by the Canadian Council of Agriculture and now included in the inspired writings of the Liberal party:
And whereas the protective tariff is the most wasteful and costly method ever designed for raising national revenue because for every dollar obtained thereby for the public treasury at least three dollars pass into the pockets of the protected interests, thereby building up a privileged class at the expense of the masses, thus making the rich richer and the poor poorer.
Let us follow the reasoning of that resolution. In the light of that statement what does the budget tell us? We have an estimated revenue this year from the tariff of 8185,000,000. For every dollar that went into the public treasury three went into the pockets of the protected interests. Multiply that by three and you have $555,000,000 which went into the pockets of the protected interests as a result of the policy of this so-called low-tariff government which we have in power to-day. Add those two amounts together and you have a total of $740,000,000 collected from the common people of Canada last year under this tariff-for-revenue policy. I saw something in the speech from the throne about the unprecedented prosperity of the Dominion. At the time I thought it was not true, but surely a country of ten millions of people that can pay that huge total in one tax must be prosperous. We now see who prospered on the national prosperity. Remember that $55,000,000 of the $740,000,000 went into the pockets of the protected interests. This government tells us they are giving us a tariff for revenue, but at the same time they say that it is the most wasteful and costly method ever designed for raising national revenue.
A studiously inclined member of this house wrote me the other day asking me a question. It. seemed that a certain colossus had appeared who could answer all tariff questions. This is the question:
What argument of the high tariff advocates do you consider the most difficult to answer, or the one which exerts the most influence on the voters?
Now, this is the strongest argument that l could furnish him. Canada is still a protectionist country. The Liberals are in power to-day; they have been in power for twenty-one years-off and on of course. The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy) told us last session that in an examination of the tariff over a period of forty years he discovered that the Liberals had reduced it four-fifths of one per cent more than had the Conservatives. What then is the argument for whioh this hon. gentleman seeks an answer? The argument to be deduced from these facts is this. Either the tariff policy introduced by Sir John A. Macdonald has been found by the Liberals to be sound political economy and good statesmanship, or else that party has been false to its own cause and to the people's trust. The Liberal party may pillory itself on either horn of the dilemma which it cares to select.
We on this side of the house do not need anybody to explain to us the virtues of the tariff. What we want is an intelligent explanation of why a party that for twenty-one years has received the votes of the people to reduce the tariff has not yet found time to begin its work. That is the kind of explanation we want. Against that argument the propaganda about tariff reductions which our friends sometimes advance are absolutely useless. I picture the Prime Minister standing up in a canoe in the straits of Gibraltar and levelling a pea-shooter at that impregnable rock. That to my mind is about what would happen -when the Liberals start to answer the argument I have just submitted to them in respect of their failure to implement their platform policies. A free-trade party? Of course. A revision-of-the-tariff-downward
The Budget-Mr. Irvine

party? Certainly. A low-tariff party? Certainly. A tariff-for-revenue party? Yes. But always "tariff" appears in the title, and the tariff is the only part implemented.
Now, there is still a chance. I do not want to close the door on hon. gentlemen opposite. I want them to make good that policy or quit. The Minister of Finance indicated that tariff arrangements were matters of international policy. That is very different from what the party stalwarts say on the hustings, but I believe it is true. The tariff policy of the United States is causing a good deal of discussion at the present time. Some of our public men are talking about reprisals, and others are talking about-nothing. I do not know whether the hon. gentlemen sitting to my right are going to advocate raising the tariff brick for brick to keep pace with any increase of the United States tariff. Instinctively and rationally I feel myself drawn away from any policy of reprisals with respect to international relations. So I will suggest to the hon. gentlemen opposite that their last and' only chance to retain the confidence of the people is to implement their low-tariff policy or get out. I would ask them now to call a conference of all the governments of the British commonwealth of nations with a view to arranging a free trade policy within the commonwealth as a means of offsetting any increase of tariff by the United States. In the first place, such a course would bind these loosely connected nations into an economic as well as a sentimental unit; in the second place, it would clearly intimate to the United States that if they want to trade with Canada they cannot do it by the tariff route; and in the third place it would reduce the cost of commodities to the Canadian people and enable them to offset the difficulties with which they would be confronted by the cutting off of the United States market to our live stock and our trade generally.
That is the suggestion which I wish to make to the hon. gentlemen opposite.
Mr. GEORGES L. DIONNE (Matane) (Translation):	Mr. Speaker, at the outset
of my remarks, I wish to sincerely congratulate the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) for the well defined, concise and pertinent speech he delivered last Friday. I must also congratulate the hon. acting leader of the opposition (Mr. Guthrie) for the splendid speech he made this afternoon. His remarks were to the point and well adapted to the circumstances.
The question of the exodus of our people to the United States was broached, the prob-

lem of unemployment, the Australian treaty, the tariff and many other questions were discussed. The exodus of people to other countries has existed ever since the world was created. The causes of this emigration are numerous; I shall, however, enumerate but a few. We find, first: a love of adventure, then a greed of gain, a craving for luxury, a longing for comforts and an inborn desire of improving one's , lot or situation. So far as this love of adventure, history records many such instances: those of Columbus,-then Cartier and later on Champlain.
Our opponents were at the helm of the affairs of this country from 1882 to 1896; they appear very favourably disposed towards the working and farming classes when they are in the opposition, they always seem to have high practical advice and means to suggest for the betterment of the workman's lot, the protection of the farming class, the development of trade and industry, but when in power they soon forget their teachings; instead of helping those poor people for whom they have so much sympathy when in opposition, they favour the autocrats and magnates of finance, the large manufacturers and the captains of industries. The exodus existed from 1882 to 1896. What did our opponents do to blot out this evil? They had every possible means at their disposal, they were in a position to entirely stamp it out, yet, I am sorry to say, they absolutely did nothing.
Now, sir, with reference to unemployment, I do not think that the tariff has any bearing on this problem, because if we glance back at early history, we note that in the time of the Pharaohs there existed years of plenty and years of scarcity. Fortunately in those days there lived the intendant Joseph who wisely provided for the lean years.
Mention was also made of the United States. The Americans are business people, industrious and they are pointed out to us as examples. But, sir, let me say that in the United States like in all countries of Europe and of the world, unemployment exists; it has always been and it will ever be so. The tariff is like the pendulum of a clock. It either moves too fast or too slow, you have the regulator adjusted and still it may be too fast or too slow. It is an easy matter to prescribe remedies but the difficulty lies in the application of the means suggested and the advice given.
From 1896 to 1911, Laurier, of cherished memory, presided over the destinies of this country. He had charge of the administration, and I must say that when he assumed

The Budget-Mr. Dionne
power in 1896, our opponents, who constantly speak of surpluses, had left but deficits!. During fifteen years, thanks to a Liberal administration, thanks to an administration of business men, these deficits were wiped out. In 1911, the people of this country, I shall not say in a moment of bewilderment, but under the influence of fear, ceased to trust the Liberals and once more confided the management of affairs to the Conservatives. It was then that we witnessed deficits again cropping up. We note that during the period which elapsed between 1911 and 1920-1921, our opponents dragged in the Great war of 1914 to 1918 to justify their expenditures. Now that they are in opposition they advocate economy, but when in power they spend with a free hand, not in the interests of the people as a whole but to favour a privileged class. I admire, sir, the courage and endurance of those brave Canadians who joined the army and went overseas to fight on the battlefields of Europe and protect the rights of allied countries; I admire the devotion to duty and the generous sacrifice of those who fought energetically and then gave their life magnanimously for their country; I have no intention of criticizing all the expenditures that were made at the time. However, our opponents who advocate economy, could have practised it then and on more than one score. They could have economized on the purchases of motortrucks and automobiles which remained in sheds in London; economy could have been practised after armistice was signed when troops were sent to Alaska for the benefit of manufacturers of army clothes and boots.
The hon. acting leader of the opposition mentioned, this afternoon, that he hoped to see a number of ministers who were free traders become protectionists. I am rather inclined to think that the hon. acting leader intends to become a convert and shows signs of it. He forsook Liberalism to join the ranks of the Conservatives. I really think his intention is to return to the fold of liberalism.
One word on protection. There is moderate and unlimited protection. Protection exists in the United States, and, it is said, that country is the most prosperous known, there are colossal fortunes, trade and industry have developed on a large scale and its population is over 100,000,000. Notwithstanding all their protection, the United States cannot prevent unemployment which exists in a great number of their cities. It is found in manufacturing centres, in industrial and commercial life.
There are periods of depression and stagnation which are uncontrollable and neither free-trade nor protection can prevent these crises.
Let me now say a few words with reference to the Australian treaty. Within the last few years butter production in this country has decreased. Our farmers export their milk and cream to the United States and our butter factories do not produce enough for the consumers of this country. What would therefore happen were this treaty cancelled? The monopolizers, the trusts would purchase all the butter made, hoard it in cold storage and hold it until the next season's output was marketed, and the new market price would regulate the scale or rather would establish the sale price of the cold storage butter and the consumer would thereby be the sufferer.
Our country is large, immense, it possesses a variety of natural resources. We are charged with exporting too many of these natural resources to the United States. But, Sir, surely a young country that does not manufacture sufficiently for all its needs, can export to other countries some of its natural products and in return import articles of consumption or utility. I am, sir, as much attached to my country as anyone else. I wish to see it happy and prosperous. When I hear our opponents express doubt as to our real prosperity, I wonder if they show political wisdom. They advocate helping agriculture and contend that the farmers are financially poor and cannot make both ends meet, balance their budget, so to speak. I am among those who advocate helping agriculture because it is the industry "par excellence," because it is an essential industry. Therefore it is quite in order to assist agriculture by every possible means, but all must participate by their energy and good will. At times, the farmers' financial situation is somewhat critical. We do not practise the sound economy of our forebears; we have not their ability to manage our affairs, too much luxury has invaded our homes. A true and infallible means to success in business-as in everything-is to leave aside subtraction and division and practise especially addition and multiplication.
Before I resume my seat, may I observe that someone has been reproaching me because I am too staunch a Liberal. I will only say this:
Though I am hot red,
Am no fanatic.
I am not a hot head
Nor a lunatic.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I wish to take this opportunity of congratulating the Liberal-Conservative party on the amendment which has been moved to the
The Budget-Mr. Church

budget. The Liberal-Conservative party is the party of progress, and it is the only party upon which the masses in this country can depend to solve economic questions. In the hour of trouble the country always sends for the Conservative party. The Conservative party has always been consistent; it believes that the industrial welfare of Canada depends on protection and safeguarding and upon the conservation of our own markets for our own products and our own work for our own workmen.
The Liberal-Conservative party to-day stands for protection; it is a protectionist party. Protection is safeguarding and safeguarding is protection. In England to-day we see the remnant of a free trade country, with a million and a quarter people out of work taking the dole. That is a fine illustration of the success of free trade. England is losing her shipbuilding orders and her industrial supremacy in coal, and the union of coal and steel is what made England the great industrial nation it became in the history of the world. The motherland is now at the parting of the ways, and with a million and a quarter civilians and returned soldiers out of work- men who fought the battles of the empire in Flanders and France-the government over there is finding it necessary to protect her industries and adopt safeguarding. So that England also is coming around to protection in what is known as the safeguarding of basic industries, such as steel, coal and many others. The economic writers whose opinions are worth considering are all agreed that safeguarding is protection, although I favour simply the old word "protection".
As I say, protection is safeguarding and safeguarding is protection; the two terms are synonymous and are interlocked, they are allied and related terms. Now it is these two protectionist doctrines that we need in Canada to-day. And no industry in this country stands more in need of the application of these doctrines than the great basic industry of agriculture. But there are other industries that need protection. The prairie provinces in a few years will become a great industrial country and it will need protection brought up to date to meet the changing conditions there from time to time. It is for that reason that we have proposed the amendment to the budget, which amendment will appeal to every farmer in and out of the house, and to every industry in the country and to those out of work. It is based on an all-Canadian tariff for Canada. I support protection as a principle not as a privilege for a few.

We have a great leader (Mr. Bennett), who we regret is not here at the moment. He is a born leader of men, a skilful manager who has devoted his life to the service of his country and his fellowman at no small sacrifice. Put him in command of the ship of state and I venture to say that the industrial ills of every province in the Dominion, from the eastern provinces where he was born all the way to the Pacific coast, would be cured and their problems solved at once.
The economic ills of Canada are to be cured by the safeguarding of industry through protection. Protection is not a dead thing; it is a living thing and is continually growing and should be brought up to date. Take the United States to-day: in the late election the issue was protection and more protection all along the line for the entire country. Both sides there were agreed on it. In that country they have built up a high tariff wall and apparently they intend to maintain that wall still higher. This is the policy of President Hoover, whom I consider one of the world's greatest economic men, a man among men. He does not mean to be unfriendly to Canada, as evidenced by the great speech he made the other day at his inauguration. He is a man who sympathizes with humanity the world over and his life has been devoted to the welfare of civilization the world over. I say, therefore, that he does not cherish any enmity towards this country, and if he proposes to protect the United States from industrial invasion that is only something to be expected. After all, it is just as fair to apply the weapon of the tariff in time of peace, when you find the industrial invader at your door taking the bread out of your workman's mouth, as it is to apply it in time' of war when the enemy is at the gates, and when you mobilize all the resources of the country to repel him. The principle of protection is the same in peace as in war for the nation as well as the individual,
I say that protection would solve the ills of the prairie provinces to-day, especially when we consider the attitude of the people of the United States. In the budget we have from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) a statement which I will discuss as far as I can in the time at my disposal. I will say this for the Minister of Finance: He is the best voting card the government has in the country today. He is a plain able business man who is very much respected not only in this house but throughout the country for his many fine qualities of head and of heart; and is a great Canadian and true Briton. I do not criticize him at all except as to his policy; while I like and admire the man I do not

The Budget-Mr. Church
like the Liberal party's policy. The liberalism we have to-day is not the liberalism of old.
I regret very much that the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. White), one of the oldest, most respected and able members of the House of Commons, has not been able to be with us this session on account of illness; I know he has been missed and we all hope he will soon return to his seat in this house with good health regained. May I add just here that I hope a general day of thanksgiving for the recovery of the king will be set apart, and I would suggest June 3, his birthday, as a proper day, when by God's grace I trust he will be fully recovered.
May I also congratulate you, Mr. Speaker, great Canadian that you are, on your lectures in France; you excelled as an ambassador of good-will. Your lectures on French history have done Canada a great deal of good in an international way for good-will in the old world. You are a great ambassador; Canada loves that glorious land of France, where so many of our own men sleep their last sleep as a result of the war; Canada adores that glorious nation towards which the eyes of the whole civilized world were turned during the war. The awful privations, the numerous trials, the untold sufferings and the terrible tribulations of the glorious French nation, surpassing anything the human imagination can conceive, will live in history as an example of the most sublime patriotism.
One of the main purposes of the budget debate is to take account of the nation's housekeeping, because after all the housekeeping in connection with an ordinary home is not very far distant in theory and method from the housekeeping in connection with a nation, and only about once a year do the representatives in parliament have a chance to discuss some of the economic ills from which the country is suffering. To-day we have a government which sits still and does nothing to cope with the economic problems of the country. Coming from an industrial constituency in Ontario I believe that the great empire province of Ontario has more economic problems to solve than all the rest of Canada, but this government seems to ignore Ontario altogether. For a long time we had not a single member of the cabinet from Ontario, 1926-7, and the present ministers representing Ontario constituencies do not seem to be sufficiently aggressive to stand up for the rights of this great province, which is paying about forty per cent of the taxes of the Dominion.
To-night the government is on trial before the bar of public opinion for their failure to govern and for their policy of laissez faire. The discussion we recently had in connection with light and power showed that our present government, as I said then, is a combination of big interests and appetites. The big interests are clamouring for more; they are weary and hungry; they are going further than they went last year and are demanding a shell-out, and the rules are to be amended to help them. To mention only a few, we have the Bell Telephone Company, the Sun Life Company, the Beauharnois power plant and all the rest, and who will stop these raids? I do not think the government will do it. During the naval debate the Liberal opposition made use of the word "gag;" now I say the rules are to be amended in order to apply "the gag" to give the big interests the right of way to what remains of the title deeds to the products of the sea, the soil, the forests and the mines of Canada. The big interests in this country such as the electric trust, the American power trust, the grain and elevator combine, the banking trust and the manufacturing trust seem to be the present masters of the administration. "Canada for the Americans" seems to be the economic policy of the government. That is shown in the government's pro-American tariff policy, in their power development policy, in their pro-American immigration policy, in their grain policy and their failure to place an embargo on hard wheat, in their failure to give adequate protection to the vegetable growers and market gardeners and their failure to apply the dumping duty, and in their separatist policy towards the rest of our empire.
To-night the government is weighed in the balance and found wanting; the unemployed asked for work in order to get bread but the government gave them a stone, together with a lot of platitudes from the head of the government. I asked a question with regard to unemployment last week but the Minister of Labour said in reply that unemployment is a question for the provinces, and from their erroneous index system say there is no unemployment. The government are being tried to-night for the way they have misgoverned; they have left undone those things which they ought to have done and they have done those things which they ought not to have done, -and there is no health in them as a government. We have had too little government from Ottawa and too much government from Washington and St. James street, including the power ring and the private millionaires of this charmed water-power circle from Mont-
The Budget-Mr. Church

real and the United States. Many of these younger power magnates hid their lights under a bushel during the Great war, staying at home and making a fortune while the men overseas were getting paid SI.10 a day.
My bill of indictment against the government includes two main counts, faults of omission and faults of commission. I charge that the faults of omission consist of twenty-six counts, as follows:
Failure to provide a policy of protection and safeguarding brought up to date to solve all the economic problems of every province.
Failure to provide a proper dumping clause.
Failure to provide some safeguards for industries.
Failure to provide a national coal and fuel policy.
Failure to bring in a policy looking to the conservation of the products of the sea, the soil, the forests and the mines for Canadians.
Failure to bring in an up-to-date Canadian Tadio policy. They fiddle along and send three favourites for a free ride around Europe while radio control is assumed by the United States.
Failure to provide a Canadian life-saving policy for the Great lakes.
Failure to provide a policy of farm relief.
Failure to implement the Duncan report in connection with steel, iron and coal.
Failure to provide for the preservation of water-powers for the people rather than for private gain and stock splits.
Failure to lay down a proper policy for the development of a greater St. Lawrence waterway as an economic necessity; this has been abandoned by the government as a waif, an orphan and an outcast.
Failure to provide an embargo on hard wheat.
Failure to deal with the question of unemployment.
Failure to lay down a policy looking to a united effort in the solution of the three great problems of empire trade, defence and migration.
Failure to provide a pro-Canadian, proBritish immigration policy.
Failure to provide any social legislation such as the extension of old age pensions and sickness and unemployment insurance.
Failure to bring in an advanced national policy on health matters.
Failure to reduce taxation, such as the income tax, the tax on cheques, the cigarette and liquor tax and other nuisance taxes.
Failure to take any taxes off the breakfast tables of the working classes.

Failure to 'bring in a national housing policy in order to help reduce the high cost of living.
Failure to make any reduction in the high cost of living.
Failure to enforce the Alien Labour Act. The Department of Labour, as I said in 1922, seems to be asleep and is one of the most useless and incompetent departments of the government to aid and protect the toiler and unemployed. Last year I asked the Minister of Labour some questions in connection with some sixty nurserymen or market gardeners who were brought to Ontario from the southern United States into York county, but I was unable to get an answer for a year.
