Then I was told that I could see the attorney general of the province, thus making a mere political football of the matter, although a federal one.
Another omission is the failure of the government to aid the maritime provinces by subsidies and subventions in connection with the steel and iron industries. Then the government failed to introduce a Pacific policy, to take care of that great empire province on the Pacific coast. They have failed to adopt a policy of closing up these wonderful embassies at Washington and Tokyo; they have failed to adopt a policy of protecting the public with insurance legislation, loan company legislation, trust company legislation and banking legislation. The working classes of this country pay millions to the insurance companies who charge anything they like, and this money is used to build up Japan, China and other countries at the expense of the Dominion.
It is time the general Insurance Act was brought up to date and revised. I do not mean to say that this legislature should fix the price of insurance, but it should give some protection to the government by having a proper audit made of these companies, and see that equitable rates are charged instead of the present prohibitive life and fire rates, to protect the policyholders.
The government gave away 'the Seven Sisters falls yesterday, and to-morrow they will be giving away the Beauhamois power site. Money has been spent in a very extravagant manner; it cost $36,000,000 to run the country when Sir Wilfrid Laurier took office in 1896, but it costs $400,000,000 to run it in 1929; they spend money like water. There has been a lack of national policy in the management of the natural resources. The government has committed these acts of omission and commission, and has failed to discover an economic policy that will assure the prosperity of Canada and make our people

The Budget-Mr. Church
happy and contented. They have no policy which will solve the country's ills. The iron, coal and agricultural industries are being left to the mercy of foreign invasion and competition. Experience shows that as the basic industries of steel and coal go, so goes the country. The government has no policy on the tariff and the conservation of our resources. They have failed to find an economic policy which will steady or maintain our prosperity, or one in which more and more of our citizens will find a share. This would create a happy and contented nation and render the people less susceptible to the preaching of radical doctrines.
We have a government to-day with no forward-looking zeal or conservative principles, and with no demonstrated capacity for public service. No single factor aids a government so much as a background of prosperity, which to a degree exists to-day but for which the government is in no way responsible. What prosperity we have to-dhy is due to the fragments of the national policy which remains in this country, to Providence and a good crop, and to the thrift, industry and sobriety of our people. We have a government of ifs and buts and doubts and fears, a government against a government, all within itself and with no leadership to solve the country's economic ills.
Have they a policy on the St. Lawrence or on the preservation of our water-powers? No. They have a policy which is here to-day and gone to-morrow; a policy which is everything by fits and starts and nothing long. They are willing to give our valuable power sites to the big interests.
Have they a policy on radio? Yes, but it is one for the Liberal party and not for the national interests. They took nearly a year to appoint a useless commission which is roaming all over Europe now doing nothing but having a good time. They have a policy of farm relief, but it is all relief and no farm. The representatives on this commission are Mr. MacLean, of Victoria, B.C., and Mr. Drury of blessed and happy memory in Ontario. The farm relief board seems to be a happy hunting ground for downtrodden politicians. Would Mr. Hoover appoint gentlemen like that? No, he would appoint an economic person who knew something about farm relief. The farm relief board consists of those with heads of all boards but they know nothing about farm relief at all or how to cure the farmers' ills.
Have they a policy on the tariff? No. They appoint a useless tariff commission to make up their minds for them. I called them 78594-49
a minstrel show. If they would tour the country as a minstrel show they would make their fortune with the interlocutor and the tambo and bones who call themselves commissioners. They are making a political football out of this tariff question while six hundred thousand Canadians have to go to the United States to try to get jobs-a tariff board of spade and shovel men whose main object is to sound the death knell of protection and industry in Canada.
Have they an immigration policy? If it is a policy it is a continental European one and not a British-born one. Have they a policy on the return of natural resources? No. The speech from the throne 1926 said that the prairie provinces were to be given their natural resources, but when the hon. member for Labelte (Mr. Bourassa) objected to that they withdrew the measure. Have they a national coal policy? No. They had reluctantly to adopt my motion therein, but they failed to carry it out. They have a policy which helps the coal barons down in Pennsylvania, for they quoted a Canadian all-rail rate of nine or ten dollars per ton for the carrying of Alberta and maritime provinces coal, and they could get no business. If they had quoted a fair rate of six dollars per ton they would have obtained the cream of the business, 'but they would rather give the business to the coal barons of the United States and make work for the people in Pennsylvania.
Have they a policy for the returned soldier? Yes, they have a policy; the returned soldier gets all the pick and shovel jobs. The good jobs and those on the bench and in the senate go to those who were willing to pay a dollar to join the Liberal association and are civilians. You see articles and advertisements in the papers in Toronto asking for second-hand clothing for the men who fought the battles of this country for $1.10 a day and for their wives and children and a tag day to help soldiers. The government takes care of these young millionaires in the Beauharnois and other power companies and the Winnipeg Electric. I know one or two of them and they never did a thing in the war. They hid their light under a bushel and made a fortune while soldiers went to war for $1.10 a day.
Have they a policy for unemployment? Mr. Vincent Massey and Herbert Marler have been taken care of. No tag day will be had to maintain their embassies. Ottawa has become the seat of a great basic industry known as the ambassador cure for unemployment. That is the policy they have in this country for unemployment while six hundred thousand

The Budget-Mr. Church

Canadians go to the United States as ambassadors at 'their own expenses looking for a job.
Have they a policy for solving the problem of British Columbia, the prairie provinces, the central provinces or the maritime provinces? No. Have they a policy which will solve the three greatest problems of empire defence namely, trade and migration? No. They went over to the colonial conference and never mentioned these problems and said Canada proposed nothing, it was satisfied.
I say the government's free-trade-wrecking tariff commission will go so far and no farther, for it is sounding the death knell of protection and industry in Canada. The government's policy has been to spend money like water and the only result will be that the labour of future generations yet unborn has been pledged for the payment of millions of dollars of interest on Canada's debt and maintenance account.
It is the duty of the government to protect the rights and prosperity, the health and comfort of its citizens. The government is sick. It looked pretty sick during the last five days when there was a discussion of the power question. It was only six votes short of defeat. The Manitoba government had to send for Doctor Hogg from Ontario and the chairman of the commission was too weak to prevent his going to Manitoba to destroy public ownership. The government of Ontario was responsible for sending Doctor Hogg to Manitoba. What did he do there? He is not a doctor at all; in fact, he has issued only one prescription in his life. He went to Manitoba and the prescription he issued electrocuted the whole Manitoba Bracken government. Before he gets through with some of the hon. gentlemen over there from Manitoba, he will electrocute them with the Seven Sisters falls in the next election, as well as the Liberal party which engaged him.
As I was saying, the government is sick; it needs a little physic. Even the Prime Minister and the cabinet on the power question were all sick of it and needed a little physic. A little tonic is often unpleasant, but it must be borne in mind that if a cure is to be effected, neither physician nor patient must flinch from taking it. So they captured a resolution or prescription the opposition gave them on water-powers.
An embargo should this session be placed on foreign products and foods that are competing unfairly with similar1 commodities produced in this country. The depression in coal is due largely to depression in trade of its best customer, the steel and iron industry.

Give them protection in Canada and you will revive those two key industries. A revival of learning is needed in the cabinet to save the country from .the tragedy of a wrecking tariff commission that is in an economic way illiterate and incapable of comprehending or of remedying economic conditions in Canada.
I am sorry there are only two front benchers present to-night. I hope I have not made the rest of the cabinet sick. No doubt they were taken very sick in the last few days when they heard the criticism of the opposition on water-powers. When they heard of so much water being used in the house during the last four or five days, no wonder they begged leave to retire and are not here to-night. Where is my hon. friend the doctor, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell), to-night? Where has he gone? Last year he became a doctor also.
Agriculture is a basic industry and requires special treatment. An embargo on hard wheat is required so as to provide work for our people in the mills in the milling of corn and flour.
As a program the budget is barren of any real progress to protect Canadians and to preserve our own markets for our own products and our own workmen. It is a very skimpy sort of chicken, a skimpy bill of fare for the working classes that fools no one. It should be committed to old mother Hubbard's cupboard so that the unemployed will see what kind of bone is in it for them. Probably that is where the balance of the cabinet have gone to-night, in order to look for the bone,-for what is left of the Liberal principles, the Liberal platform laid down in the city of Ottawa a few years ago. The budget is a full chicken with the bone out of it for the rich but the masses get not even a good bone. Shorn of a lot of its fads and frills, it contains nothing that will benefit the masses of the country. I admit the government have taken twenty-five cents off the expense of the tickets to which a member of parliament is put in coming to and going from Ottawa. That is one of the few things they have thrown over here. One thing I am sure we cannot do is blame the lord high executioner of the government, the Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot), for whom I have a great deal of respect, for having any part in its draftsmanship, because there is nothing in it to execute and no one to execute except the taxpayer.
What do the Liberal prohibitionist supporters of the government .think of the way in which the government has played with the rum-running business and allowed the United

The Budget-Mr. Church
States to violate a number of international treaties and have armed gunboats on the lakes? One thing left out of the budget is any instruction to the workers how they should spend' their money, because the workers have no money to spend and because of the economic policy of the government many of them are out of work. We have to have a tag day for the soldiers in distress, but no tag day is needed for the maintenance of our ambassadors at Tokyo and Washington. If the government's budget is cut up into parts, it is a program of shin plasters for the rich and a committal to the poorhouse for the unemployed and the poor. Where is and what is the government's tariff policy? If we are to judge by the mock trials held by those delightful busybodies, the tariff commission, it may be summed up under two heads as follows:
(a)	That nothing that can be bought in the United States shall be made in Canada, and,
(b)	That everything that cannot be bought in the United States shall be imported from overseas, from Europe, preferably from Germany.
The government turns a deaf ear to any adequate dumping clause even though some of their own supporters ask for it in the house.
The great industrial system of the United States was built up on protection. President Hoover will yet drive Canada to erect a similar wall and adopt a self-respecting reciprocal policy. Canada can no longer continue to buy $900,000,000 worth of high-priced manufactured goods from the United States, nfearly two-thirds of which could be manufactured in Canada, and pay for that $900,000,000 worth out of her raw material. We require a proper and adequate reciprocal treaty. The government will not insert in the tariff a clause to tell the United States so. Mr. Hoover is a business man and as business is business among individuals as well as nations, he would not object to it. The Monroe note and the Kellogg note mean nothing, but if the government would write a note along the lines I have suggested, they might accomplish something. As I said in the session of 1926-7:
In the days of Horace Greeley opportunities for employment in the United States were threatened by imports from Europe. To-day opportunities for employment in Canada are threatened by imports from the United States. The United States did not require the fqunders of American industry to go before a tariff commission to persuade the commissioners that the tariff should be so changed that their industries would be able to employ Americans in their own country instead of driving them to seek employment in foreign lands. Nero never fiddled while Rome burned the way this government is 78594-494
fiddling in appointing a tariff commission to solve the economic problems of this country. Instead of announcing in the budget some measure of protection and safeguarding legislation that would solve our economic ills, nothing is being done by the government to relieve our unemployed who are asking for a job that they may get bread. Many industries are closed up altogether, others are working only fifty per cent, and even the great agricultural industry of the west is suffering.
This wonderful government which continues its policy of the ambassador cure for unemployment dooms 600,000 other Canadians to appoint themselves ambassadors at their own expense to search in a foreign land, the United States, for the jobs that they cannot find in their own country. In the days of Horace Greely opportunities for employment in the United States were threatened by imports from Europe as the opportunity to-day for employment in Canada is threatened by imports from the United States. The Americans from 184960 asked their rulers for the bread of employment. These rulers did not offer their countrymen the stone of free trade theory and the platitudes of a pro-American tariff and an economic policy of laissez faire. No, and these rulers did not require the founders of American industry to go before a minstrel show of a tariff commission and persuade the interlocutor, the tambo and the bones who call themselves commissioners, that the tariff should be changed in favour of industries that would employ Americans in their own country instead of driving these Americans, as Canadians are being driven, to seek employment in a foreign country.
The government's tariff policy has made it impossible for the workers to obtain the full product of their labour or a full dinner pail. The government never was and never will be a working class government or a government representing all sections of the country.
This budget would make a great crazy quilt for the Minister of Agriculture to raffle off at a fall fair and! throw dm with it a free prescription or two as well seeing that he has now a doctor's degree. The budget is an enigma, a Chinese puzzle; it means nothing, and will lead to nothing of economic benefit to the country; it will do nothing to better conditions and provide work for Canadians in any of the provinces. It is just a smoke-screen thrown over the economic ills with which the country is afflicted. The budget is a neat apology for the government's failure to govern and for its failure to shift the burden of taxation from the toilers and the fawners to the rich and those more able to pay. It is not even a platform to stand on, let alone one to get in on. It is a mixed! grill kind of tariff, and no all-
?72
The Budget-Mr. Church

Canadian tariff a.t ail. It is only an academic thesis of several resolutions, platitudes, evasions, and excuses for turning over what remains of industry to our competitors; to the Americans and other foreign manufacturers at the expense of Canadian workmen. There can be no definite criticism from the opposition because there is really nothing in the budget to criticize.
The first cornerstone of an Immigration policy is to keep our own in Canada. The second great essential is to provide work for Canadians at present in this country, but the government proposes nothing to attain that end. The government have shown themselves incapable of bringing forth any legislation which will help solve the problems facing us and relieve conditions which exist all over the country. There is no adequate protection for industry. There is no social legislation in the way of an adequate and up-to-date pension scheme or some system of unemployed insurance. There is no social legislation for the workers in this budget. Many of the toilers in the old country are out of work. People over there got tired of the party system, and they formed the Labour party. And now all the old and new parties in England are in favour of social1 legislation. We should adopt social legislation in this country adapted to our finances and to our circumstances, If we had a little more practical religion and loved our neighbours as ourselves, this house would not prorogue until the soldiers and their dependents were all properly looked after. We would see that none of God's creatures in Canada who were willing to work were denied the means of earning their livelihood. We would abolish slums; we would solve the housing problem; we would give every main, woman and child in this country a chance to live and exist in a free country as God's creatures.
We require in this country a national policy of health. The cost of sickness in Canada is computed at $311,000,000 a year, eighty-nine per cent of which is a direct charge upon 'the individual. The loss of future earnings through premature death is conservatively estimated at $1,000,000,000 a year, so that $1,311,000,000 is the price paid for illness and its results in Canada each year. The health of the people is left, under the British North America Act, to the Dominion, hnd we need a national health policy in this country. In York county, $12.50 a head is spent on education, contrasted with 19 cents per head for public health. This is because the public asks for education, but they have not yet been able to see the value of public health. In England they have had a British board of health since 1831, as a 
department of the government. That has now developed into the ministry of health, one of the most efficient in the world. In this country we have only had a ministry of health a very short time, since 1927. As an example of what might be done, I might point out that in the year- 1925, 30,000 people in the United States died of influenza, 90,000 of tuberculosis, and over 95,000 of cancer. The government will spend $2,000,000 to prevent deaths at level crossings, but very little in the war against disease. The time has come for a national health policy, and millions should be spent in it. Let the government economize on something else of a material nature instead of on something which is at the cost of the lives of our people.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, fortunate is the hon. member who follows in debate our most estimable friend from Toronto Northwest (Mr. Church). I find, nothing to criticize in what he says.
Turning to the address that was made this afternoon by the acting leader of the opposition (Mr. Guthrie), we all remember the critical times in this house nine or ten years ago when we were fighting over the question of public or private ownership of the railways. We were then sitting to the left of the Speaker, and on both sides of the house were found men in support of one policy or the other. We all remember the attitude of the then Minister of Railways, now sitting in the senate. The greatest critic of public ownership of the railways in the house at that time was the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill), and surely he knew railways. We were all more or less skeptical as to the success of the railways under public ownership and administration. We remembered how on the old Intercolonial two-thirds of the passengers travelled without buying tickets, and naturally we who are now sitting on this 6ide of the house were skeptical as to what would happen to the railways so long as the Conservative government was in power. We knew there would be no management worth mentioning so long as the Conservatives were in power. But when the Liberal government came into office, they searched the whole world over and found in Sir Henry Thornton the greatest railway man available, the greatest that could be found in this universe, and undoubtedly he has made an outstanding success in the management of the national system. He would not undertake the management Until the government had promised him a free hand in the management of the road. He sought and obtained the loyal cooperation of every employee of the system,

The Budget-Mr. Baldwin
and under his management the road has progressed until it is now one of the greatest railway systems in the world. The railway committee may be of use to the presidents of the two great railway systems in this country, but personally I would trust Mr. E. W. Beatty, president of the Canadian Pacific, and Sir Henry Thornton, president of the Canadian National, to extend their lines anywhere they saw fit, because I believe they are both men of outstanding ability. Anyone who has travelled extensively must know that the two great railway systems in this country are the equal of any in the world.
The acting leader of the opposition went on to say, in effect, that this government was spending money like drunken sailors, and he condemned them especially for spending money on public works. We all know that during the war, from motives of economy, buildings were not properly maintained, and the result was that public buildings, wharves, and the like, got into a bad state of repair and needed painting inside and out. It is not prudent to allow public property to decay and tumble down, and it was necessary for the government to spend money to put the public works of this country in decent repair.
The acting leader of the opposition assailed the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) in regard to the dairying industry. I should like to tell this house that the Minister _ of Agriculture has done more for the dairying industry than any other minister of agriculture since confederation. He worked for two years trying to prevent oleomargarine from being imported and sold in Canada. Before its sale was prohibited, you could buy butter much cheaper than you can to-day. If my memory serves me a right-and it is retentive-the leader of the opposition voted against the repeal of the oleomargarine law. But the ex-Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Tolmie), now Premier of British Columbia, Donald Sutherland and three others assisted us through two sessions of parliament in fighting and repealing that law. By that action we did more for the farmers of Canada than has been effected by any other legislation passed by this house. To-day butter is fifty cents a pound. Is that not a sufficiently high price for the labouring man to pay?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Last session the Australian treaty was freely criticized, mainly on the score of the importations of butter from that country, but I have not heard any specific objections so far this session. Then the leader of the opposition assailed business conditions in general. He said the labouring men cannot get work, the farmers have nothing to do. I want to tell you, Mr. Speaker, that a company with which I am connected has brought industries into the eastern townships in the last nine years which industries in buildings and plant have spent $37,500,000, and annually they are paying in wages $5,200,000. Since I heard the hon. gentleman's speech I have received a letter from home. The manager of the small business that has been in my family for the past 120 years wrote me to say that he could not get help to start our mill, the people were so busy. That is typical all over the eastern townships. I happen to be in Montreal pretty often. The hon. leader of the opposition stated that there were a lot of people running around Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg and Vancouver looking for work. Well, I have not noticed that in Montreal, but it may be that those people belong to that class which hunts for work and prays it wont find any. Nor have I heard of any soup kitchens. He mentioned something about money being collected to help the poor. Well, the poor we shall have with us always, as Scripture tells us.
Then my hon. friend attacked our ambassadorial homes in Washington and London, but I noticed there was not a word about the .Scribe hotel. For two or three sessions we were told that the Scribe hotel was one of the greatest scandals in the history of this country. Well, I think the silence of the opposition proves that the Scribe hotel has been a very successful investment. That is why they have dropped the subject. My good friend from Toronto Northwest, mentioned the appointment to the Tokyo embassy. I am pleased that a gentleman from Stanstead county is to represent Canada in that wonderful country, and I am sure the appointment will be justified by the able maner in which our ambassador there will look after Canadian interests. And I think Mr. Massey in Washington is worth to Canada all and more than we are paying him.
With regard to the tariff, boys of my age and a long time before remember that ever since the abrogation by the United States of
The Budget-Mr. Baldwin

the reciprocity treaty in natural products the Conservative party has worked assiduously for its revival. It is useless for me to remind the house that members of Conservative governments from time to time have made more visits to Washington in an attempt to negotiate a treaty for reciprocity in natural products than have the members of Liberal governments. It was not until 1911 that the Conservative party made a change of front and thanks to their flag-waving campaign the country then pronounced itself emphatically against reciprocity with the United States. I believe that if you can have reciprocity equivalent to free trade in natural products it would be all right. But I am a protectionist-an adequate protectionist. I like to look after myself. Self-preservation is a mighty good thing in personal matters, in family matters, in county matters and in national matters.
I believe that we have men on the treasury benches who are big enough to cope with any problem, tariff or otherwise. It has been stated by some of the most prominent mem in Montreal that the Beauharmois undertaking would result in a defeat of the government. Now, when I listened to my great chief- great? Yes, just as great as any prime minister 'that ever stood on the floor of this house-when- I heard him map out that triune conference between Ontario, Quebec and the federal government, and his statement that when in that proposed conference they agree on a policy that will suit all parties, then, and not until then, will they resume conferences with 'the United States. To my mind, that is business.
There seems to be a spirit of fellowship between the other side of the house and this. I have to congratulate the leader of the opposition on having made one of the most comprehensive speeches ever made in this house, but the longer you are on your feet the more you lay yourself open to criticism, and I venture to say that in due time his arguments will be answered satisfactorily to the membere on this side. I have not the least doubt.
Now, Canada is a wonderful and amazing country. If we do not know it, let us visit other parts of the globe and we shall realize how the world regards us. I have n>o fault to find with the member for Frontenac-Addington (Mr. Edwards), but if ever I was surprised by any proceeding in this house it was by his attack on the Minister of the Interior last year. The big Scotch head of the minister is full of common sense; and the best science in the world is the science of 
common sense, or horse sense. Now, then, the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. McRae) elaborated a plan of settlement on a large scale. But it was too expensive. Then a conference of all parties was held, but the great question of filling up our open spaces was not solved. But I think we must acknowledge our Minister of the Interior is a great man, for he did his utmost to make that conference a success. Our great railway systems and other organizations are doing all they can to attract immigrants. Personally I would give very little money to bring people into Canada. If every man and woman, boy and girl, whether at home or abroad, would tell the world what a wonderful country we have here, that would be the best kind of publicity; and if they feel they have not sufficient scope, let them talk of the Great British Empire. There is nothing that makes me shrink with such despair as to hear our boys and girls talking about going to the United States. My business takes me from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and occasionally into the United States, and I know of cities there, with a population of half a million, where the people are talking treason and rebellion and what not. Let a man say that he is from some part of the British Empire and those people will say, "You come from the finest country in the world, where honour and justice prevail". We do not see ourselves as others see us, and I can assure you that there are any number of people in the United States who will readily admit that we have an amazing country in this Dominion. They would come here and buy up every stock outright, our bank stocks, industrials, hydro-electric and everything else, if we let them. But our population, composed of English, Scotch, Irish and French, knows how to take care of itself.
We need patriotism in this country, and this government is doing all in its power to promote harmony among the various classes in Canada. I admire the genuine spirit of fellowship which has been displayed here in the past, day or two in settling a great question which has been the subject of considerable debate in the house. The Canadian people are coming more and more to realize the greatness of their country. We are far better off than they are in the United States, if only we will all work together. There you find a population of some fifteen million negroes, and still further south in Mexico you find a terrible and pugnacious people. So far as labour is concerned, we have room for all those who wish to come in. An appreciable distance west of the Mississippi you will find labour of

The Budget-Mr. Baldwin
the class we have not in Canada, and on the Pacific coast there are crowds of Chinese, Japanese, and Mexicans. These people work seven days in the week and they work like Trojans. For my part I have nothing against them, and in this regard my views are well known; it will be found in many volumes of Hansard. I would let everyone come in who was law-abiding and willing to work, because I am not very strong on the colour line, for the simple reason that this climate will not attract the coloured races in great numbers.
I have spoken many times regarding the West Indies, and I firmly maintain that we should have political union with that section of the empire. As a result of the part we played in the war, we have a tremendous debt. Why, therefore, should not Great Britain acknowledge the right of Canada to have something for her sacrifice of life and money? And there is nothing at all unreasonable in the proposal. Take the United States:	they
have added as much territory to their domain as they had sixty-five years ago. Now they have Cuba, Porto Rico and other places, and the annexation has proved beneficial to both parties. If Canada could annex the British West Indies it would be a good thing not only for the West Indies themselves but for this country as well. The same thing applies to Newfoundland, where there are water-powers and other resources that could be developed advantageously. Certainly I believe that an arrangement could be arrived at between Canada on the one hand and the British West Indies and the mother country on the other, whereby we could have a very helpful political union. The method of representation of the West Indies in this parliament could be worked out; possibly they could have representatives in the senate. There are only two and a half million people in the British West Indies and there should be no difficulty in arranging this union. True, their skins are dark, but I am sure that no one would compare them with the coloured population of the United States. Booker T. Washington was, of course, a great man, and he was educated to some extent along high ideals. But I do not think that the coloured population of the United States, taken altogether, could compare with the people of the West Indies. I have attended conferences in Canada at which there were representatives from the British West Indies and I am bound to say I never heard more capable speakers. They also speak with a very pleasing accent. So far as I can see, therefore, there is no
obstacle in the way of a political union between Canada and that promising part of the empire.
I would not offer very much assistance in the way of money as an inducement to get people to come to this country. In my opinion that is absolutely ridiculous. Let us make it known throughout the world that this is one of the greatest countries to which any man could come who was looking for an opportunity to make his way in life. Do not let us entertain any prejudices against some of the excellent European peoples merely because we happen to have fought against them some years ago. I do not want to say anything to hurt the feelings of anyone, but I may remark that during the war the people of one of the finest countries in the world, the Germans, were unduly criticized. Right in these benches in the Union government anyone who had a drop of German blood in his veins was regarded as a murderer. But some of the most progressive, some of the richest states in the American union are settled by these people. Take Wisconsin and Minnesota for instance: some of the richest sections in those states are peopled by Norwegians, Germans and immigrants from Sweden. I would have no barriers against immigration into Canada. I have seen people pouring into New York by the thousand, and I see no reason why they should be shut out. It is a good deal like fencing out sheep when some have tasted the pasture on the other side. You may build your fence as high as you like, but some leader will find his way through and others will follow. I have no doubt that many people are getting into the United States from Canada through the international border. Young men go there in search of work and after applying for one job after another they finally take to the shovel and spade. Then they are glad enough to come back to Canada; and they come back singing, "Home, Sweet Home." Tens of thousands of people who go there are forced to come back. If I were in charge of affairs in the United States and I had a lot of disgruntled people in the east and middle west to deal with, I would give them free transportation to the arid belt.
In the United States they have their troubles; the automobile has destroyed them; they have the curse and cancer of divorce. In Los Angeles nearly 5,000 divorces are granted each year and at Reno, Nevada, it is a daily occurrence. A man sees some little butterfly on the Street and thinks what a wonderful time he would have if she were his wife, but if he gets her he probably
The Budget-Mr. Baldwin

has to darn his own socks and get his own breakfast, and if he has any money in his pockets she gets it when he goes to sleep. They have a great many things in the United States, but we must remember that the courts of Los Angeles are running every day of the week except Sunday; they have a seventeen story jail there and all the prisons are filled to overflowing. I have considerable property in the United States which I am willing to sell at any price. If you sell a farm in the United States the purchaser will not farm it; he may raise a few potatoes, but they are no more fit to eat than are green bananas, and I would much prefer a good Irish potato raised here in Canada. We have an example of what the Irish potato has done; look at that good old Irish race. They say the Irishmen did not know how to run their own country, but if you go to any part of the world you will find Irishmen helping to run almost every other country. I was in Louisiana shortly after Governor Long had been elected; he is an Irishman. The amount of money in the United States is perfectly amazing, but we must remember that in order to make that money the United States made a terrible sacrifice of human life. If I had been Stanley Baldwin instead of Billy Baldwin, when the delegation went to the United States to settle the war debt I would have said, " This settlement shall be contingent upon France, Italy, Germany and Russia paying their debts to us; if they default we will default also." Then we would have had the moral support of the United States in collecting those debts. Great Britain has been the greatest colonizing power the world has ever known and has done more for civilization than any other nation. You will remember that in his inaugural speech President Hoover said the United States was a cosmopolitan nation made up of all peoples of the world, but only one nation gave them their language. We know the country to which he referred, and I consider that a great compliment. If we must ape the United States, let us take her best features and leave her worst; then we will make great progress, because that country has a great many splendid things about it, but we should inform our young men and women that if they go to the United States to look for work they have not one chance in fifteen of becoming successful in comparison to the chances they have here in Canada.
Are our fathers and mothers doing their duty in this country? I think not. When I was a boy there was more love of country, more patriotism and more talk of Canada and the British Empire than we hear now. Nowadays everyone is busy trying to make money; 
we are making money, but the man who can make money and still keep his head is rare. Has anyone ever thought just what one good labouring man means to a country? You cannot compute it, so we should make every effort to keep these people, their children and their children's children in this country. My best friends, and those for whom I would do the most, are those who earn their daily bread, who do it cheerfully and make play of their work.

speechtext:
I think there are quite
a number of people in this country who do not earn their bread. Under our present system when a man commits a crime we put him in gaol; while he is there he spends his time thinking up what deviltry he will do when he gets out. I would make every man in gaol work until he would be glad to go to bed; I would treat him fairly well and perhaps pay him something for his work, but a country that keeps its prisoners in idleness makes a great mistake. I undesrtand that prisoners are not now allowed to work and I consider that very wrong; people who are sent to jail should leave after serving their sentences better men and women than when they went to jail. Last year it was proposed to lash a prisoner when he entered gaol and to lash him when he left; would that sort of thing make a good man out of him? These people can be made into good citizens; in the United States the prisoners farm large areas of land, and when these people have served their sentences and return to society they are respected by their neighbours. That is as it should be; I presume there are just as good people in gaol as are out of it.
I have found wonderful Jewish lawyers in New York, Chicago and Los Angeles-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure we have listened to a splendid defence of the Robb budget. At the time that budget was delivered I thought it had some very good points in that it was clear, short and concise, but after our acting leader of the opposition (Mr. Guthrie) analysed it this afternoon I discovered there was something very much wrong with it. I am sure that every member of the house will congratulate the acting leader of the opposition upon his splendid budget criticism. I have heard compliments from both sides of the house and from all groups, on its being one of the best speeches delivered in the house for many, many years. When the acting leader of the opposition had completed his exposition of the government and the members composing it, I felt that we must have some doubt in our minds as to the opinion expressed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) at the beginning of the session During the early days of the session, when he was reminded that the prosperity of the country was in some measure due to the gifts of a kindly Providenoe, he pointed out that Providence must act through men and governments. He was not willing at all to give the credit to Providence for any part of our prosperity, but according to him it must be due to a combination of "Me und Gott."
I should like to remind the house that Providence is associated in a very peculiar way with this government. For example, one year ago the Prime Minister brought to our notice the case of many aged, dependent citizens of the country and the government introduced a policy of old age pensions. I can hear the Minister of Labour (Mr. Keenan), that kindly hearted Canadian citizen, speaking to the numerous audiences he has addressed and those he will address in the future of the beneficence of the Prime Minister who has so carefully provided, in association with a kindly Providence, for our aged and dependent citizens. But what must the good Providenoe feel like when, at this early date after the passage of that great measure, the Prime Minister pronounces this
778	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Ross (Kingston)
beneficent act coming from this government as a "vicious policy"? This is only one example of the actions of the men in this government with whom Providence has to act. If you want to picture Providence acting with men and governments as the Prime Minister said, picture it acting now through the kindly heart of the Postmaster General (Mr. Yeniot) in a policy of execution of postmasters. Picture Providence cooperating with the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) in his trip of economy through Europe taking along with him a government car and a government chauffeur.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
"What have you to say
about it?"

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have nothing to
say about it. I am sure he has made the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Elliott) jealous that he cannot visit those places in Europe, for instance, the beautiful resorts of France. If the Minister of Agriculture had taken a government car and made a trip to the Holy Land where he might have been reminded of his sins of past days, I might have found some excuse for his trip with a government car and chauffeur.
On that occasion there was a second statement made by the Prime Minister, namely, that the prosperity was due to the policy brought in by the Robb budget. I have searched for a policy in the budget and even in the address and I can find no statement of a national policy of any kind that this country can build upon or look to with any hope. If there is one I should like to know it. If I were to pick out a policy that would mark this government, I would say that it had a policy of beautification. The government has set about to beautify this capital. I think the object was that people coming to the capital would be able to view from the great confederation square these magnificent buildings, but if one Should go down on that so-called confederation square to-day where there has been so much destruction, and endeavour to get a view of these beautiful buildings, he would have to be cross-eyed to see them. They have beautified the capital of the United States to the extent of about $500,000; they have beautified the capital of Great Britain to the extent of more than a million dollars; they have yet to beautify the capital of Japan and the capital of France. When they get through with that, they will start on a policy of beautification of these great ambassadors of ours. One in Washington is already beautified and we are waiting with some interest to see what the beautiful adornment of

this great minister to Tokyo will be. In fact the only policy of the government is that of a beauty parlour.
Turning to the Robb budget, so-called, as I have said it has merit. It has described in a simple way expenditures and revenues. There is nothing new in that. It has described our public debt. Our leader has dealt with those matters which are of financial importance and I am going to pass them by. It showed that we have a certain amount of prosperity. Everyone will admit that the country is prosperous; it cannot help being prosperous. While I admit there are some merits in the budget, I fail to find in it or the address which has been passed'-because these two things combined should place before us the policy of the government and show us what is intended for the future-any effort on the part of the government to care for the people of Canada. You might say that they constitute rather a failure to provide. I would go further and say that the budget was well named in being called a Robb budget because we find that the result of the several Robb budgets that have been brought down is that they are robbing the country of certain factors we should have.
We can picture the prosperity of Canada. The 'Minister of Finance might well speak of all that the country now has and will have, of its possibilities in the making of a happy and contented people, of the attractions that we have to draw people to it, of the possibilities of establishing and building up great industries, and also of making a happy and contented agricultural people; and yet I can find nothing of that in the budget. The Minister of Finance and every minister on the government benches must admit that in spite of all our prosperity, in spite of all our possibilities, in spite of all that this country has in the way of resources, too many people are leaving Canada. Surely there must be some way to remedy this situation. The report of the United States Commissioner of Immigration shows that last year we lost some 73,963 people to the United States. Of that number we lost from .the province of Quebec 17,963. I can imagine some member of the government rising in his place and answering: Oh, yes, but the number is decreasing year by year. Is that due to any policy of this government? Is it due to any one of the Robb budgets? Not one bit. Let me read to you what the United States Commissioner of Immigration says with respect to this matter:
Immigration from Canada has decreased from year to year since the present quota law became effective July 1, 1924.

The Budget-Mr. Ross (Kingston)
It was in, 1924 that we had the first tinkering with the tariff, and in that year some 200,090 people left this country. But in 1925, following the introduction of the United States visa law, which compelled everyone leaving this country and entering the United States to pay $8 per head, there was a decrease, and no wonder; but it was not due to any policy which this government had put in force; it was due to the law which the United States government had put into effect to prevent the great flow of people across the line from this country resulting from the policies initiated and brought into force by this government.
There are other factors connected with the immigration from this country of 73,000 people which are more important still, and which show that the successive Robb budgets are continually robbing us of something which cannot be measured in dollars and cents. Of the
73,000	who left this country, 11,009 were under sixteen years of age; 17,045 were between sixteen and twenty-one years; 21,000 were between twenty-two and twenty-nine; 10,000 were between thirty and thirty-seven; 5,000 between thirty-eight and forty-four; 8,000 between forty-five and fifty-five. In other words we are losing to the United States the best that this country produces, the young people; for of this 73,000 we find that 28,000 were under the age of twenty-one. So perhaps the Robb budget is well named, because we are losing our most valuable assets, the young people of this country.
The budgets that we have had for the last three or four years also show that we are acting in a very unreasonable way in another respect. I should like to draw the attention of the house to a few facts regarding our imports and exports; and by the way, I am shortening my remarks on this phase because our leader dealt so ably with this subject this afternoon. Here are a few facts I have taken from the trade reports of this country, from which we can assuredly draw some useful lessons; and I am going to put them to the house in a way that appears interesting to me. In 1927 there were imported into this country $12,160,529 worth of engines, boilers and locomotives. No one will deny that we can and do manufacture these articles in Canada, yet we imported them in 1927 to the amount I have stated. If these figures of importation were continually decreasing we might say that the government was doing something, but on the contrary our imports are constantly rising. In 1928, engines, boilers and locomotives were imported into this country to the value of $13,559,000. Of rolling mill products-
I am selecting these items because they affect very considerably the small cities and towns along our frontier-we imported in 1927, 834,000,000; 1928, $44,000,000; tools, 1927, $1,800,000; 192,8, $2,238,000; wool and its products, an article that should not be found in our imports, in 1927, $34,000,000 and in 1928, $38,000,000 worth; of textile products, in 1927, $14,000,000; in 1928, $15,000,000; milk and its products, in 1927, $2,700,000; 1928, $3,194,000 worth.
Now, turning to the other side, what do we find in the way of exports of similar goods? In 1927 we exported $8,700,000 worth of textiles, and in 1928, $7,600,000 worth; of animal products, in 1927, $128,000,000; 1928, $126,000,000; of rolling mills products, 1927, $1,- 600,000; 1928, $862,000; of farm machinery and implements, 1927, $11,000,000; 1928, $10,000,000.
Under the policies that have been brought into force by this government you will notice that in each one of these lines our imports are increasing each year and our exports decreasing. Surely the lesson is plain. Placing these import and export figures side by side, we see that during the life of this government our imports under the Robb budgets have been increasing each year, and our exports decreasing. What does that mean? It means less work in Canada and more work in the United States and other countries; and it is for these reasons that our young people, the working people of this country, are leaving for the United States, as many of them as can pay their $8 head tax and get out.
Three years ago I followed this same line and I pointed to information given to me by experienced superintendents of factories and experienced workmen to the effect that if we manufactured in this country, as we could, the goods we are importing, there would be work for 74,000 more people in this country. Based on the ordinary family we would have in the neighbourhood of three hundred thousand more people if a different policy had been adopted. Now with the increase that is taking place I am satisfied that we would have four hundred thousand more people working here under those circumstances.
I go still further. Since the introduction of the Robb budget and the treaties that followed we are affected in a similar way along other lines. To-day our leader gave figures of the importations of Australian and New Zealand butter. I am not going to deal with the subject because others better qualified to speak from the agricultural point of view will discuss it; but I want to point out to the government something that is taking
780	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Ross (Kingston)
place at the present time. Last year and the year before you could go into any grocery store in this and other cities and towns and buy over the counter Australian and New Zealand butter. To-day if a member of this house went to any of those stores and asked for a pound of Australian or New Zealand butter he would be told there was none available. But you can buy butter at those stores which I am told any person who has had experience can detect at once to be New Zealand or Australian butter. An injustice is being done our dairy farmers, and I should like the Minister of Agriculture to solve the mystery. Undoubtedly a double robbery is taking place: the agriculturist is robbed of his home market, which he is entitled to; and, if what I suspect is going on, the consumer also is being robbed, for he is paying from three to four cents a pound more for that mislabelled butter than if it were sold for what it really is-New Zealand butter. Notwithstanding this apparent absence of Australian and New Zealand butter our importations are increasing. I think this should engage the attention of the Minister of Agriculture and his colleagues.
By way of emphasizing and demonstrating the fact that the government are providing work for our friends across the line to the detriment of Canadian interests, I desire to bring to their attention a matter which is very generally discussed among those engaged in shipping on the great lakes. As is well known, our coastal law prevents American boats trading between Canadian ports, but by order in council they have been allowed to unload their cargo at a Canadian port provided they do not return to the Canadian head of the lakes for a second cargo. Nevertheless they have evaded the law and returned with another cargo. This has been drawn to the attention of the government for some time, and the lack of any action on their part forces one to tlhe conclusion that, in a way, they favour American interests to the detriment of Canadian. During the past summer it was repeatedly drawn to the attention of the government that American boats were unloading grain and returning to the Canadian read of the lakes for a second cargo. If this was a matter of urgency and expediency, well and good; but it is not. This practice works to the detriment of Canadian labour and Canadian shipping interests. When the government could give no satisfactory answer as to whether or not this practice was to continue, I sent the following telegram to the Commissioner of Customs at Ottawa: 
Understand United States vessels loading storage cargoes of grain at Canadian ports under order in council 1599 and have unloaded at Canadian ports in Georgian bay and at Port Colborne, and returned for second cargo at Canadian head of lakes. Will you please state whether this is done in violation of the statute and order in council, or whether special permission was given, and iif so whether given by further order in council. Vessels named so far are Berwind and Charles Hutchinson, but others are following. Please telegraph and confirm with full particulars.
In reply I received the following telegram:
Order in council provide that certain vessels may load grain for winter storage and unload such cargo at Canadian or United States port on resumption of navigation next spring, or unload at shipper's option at any such ports on or before opening of navigation next year. There is reasonable ground for the shippers to believe that the provisions of the order in council have not been violated.
Again we telegraphed that this practice was going on to the disadvantage of Canadian shippers, Canadian working men and Canadian homes. What was the answer? I ask hon. members to pay attention to this telegram from the Commissioner of Customs:
Order in council was not passed on recommendation of minister of this department, and the department considers order in council permitted action which has taken place.
Does this mean that this divinely chosen body of administrators are not acting in cooperation, that the minister of one department can have an order in council passed which will violate the principles of another department, or that one minister is not in touch with his colleagues? The whole procedure savours of favoritism to our friends to the south, to the disadvantage of Canadian commercial interests. It may be that the government has a sufficient answer, but in the meantime commercial interests have suffered, not only for one season but for several, and Canadian bottoms which are doing their best to give a satisfactory service are being discriminated against in favour of American boats.

speechtext: We have asked for the new order in council permitting it, if there is any. It has been drawn to the attention of the government not once but many times. If the practice has been carried on for a great many years, surely the minister will admit that it is time to stop it.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I admit that what the hon. member says is quite true. It is a very old practice each fall for the shippers of grain to request the privilege of allowing American bottoms to store winter grain. Permission has always been granted by special order in council each fall. I agree with my hon. friend that Canadian shipping men have almost every year of which I have found a record protested as my hon. friend is protesting to-night. I have no objection to the protest. It is only a question of judgment whether it is wise to continue to allow that winter storage.

The minister knows as well as I do, however, that it is a violation of the law for these boats to go back and get another cargo. There is where the Canadian law is violated.

If this is a divinely chosen body cooperating with Providence, as the Prime Minister tells us, to produce prosperity in this country, and they do not know after a dozen telegrams or so, then I do not know how much we can assign to Providence and how much to the men in the government.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have endeavoured to bring forward some new matters and I have gone into a fairly complete analysis of them. But let me say this before I sit down. While we say that the budget has done some good, we contend that there is displayed in the budget and in the policy of the government a total disregard for the development of this country. There is a total want of care or interest in providing work in this country, and I have shown that if we were to adopt a policy of the kind I have indicated we could save millions and have a greater population. In the budget which has been brought down one cannot help feeling just as our good friend from Stanstead (Mr. Baldwin) feels, in treating things: why take a little bit of a bite? The governement have made out of this sales tax now enough money to represent all the reduction in the debt. If the sales tax had been properly administered, if it had been properly arranged, it would have been a good thing. It was intended that the sales tax should guard against an excessive expenditure of money in this country. But it has not been administered along that line; it has not been used for that purpose. And the government, I repeat, have already made out of the sales tax enough money to equal every bit of surplus they have had in the past. The time has come, therefore, when this parliament should take a firm stand and say that instead of taking off a cent or half a cent or a quarter the government should abolish the sales tax.
The government have merely taken off two or three little things that they themselves put on. They put on these extra nuisance taxes. They criticized the old sales tax, but when they came in they imposed a heavier sales tax. Now the time has come, I say, when instead of taking off that little bit we should insist that the Minister of Finance abolish the whole thing and throw it into the scrap can.
There is another feature in which there is unfair treatment. The government have made a great ado about changes in postage. Sometimes these changes are put through in the budget and sometimes by order of the Great Executioner. At any rate, they are little bits of things. But the minister is yet holding over the cities that little war tax on postage, and I think the time has now come when he should decide to put back the postage in the city to what it was in pre-war days, just as it is in all other parts of Canada.
It seems to me that this budget, or any other budget, should pronounce some definite policy of debt reduction. I believe the Minister of Finance, in regard to interest and refunding, got his only hint from the speech
782	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Ross (Kingston)
-the only constructive speech-delivered by the hon. member for Toronto East Centre (Mr. Matthews). Following that speech there was a little bit of refunding and saving of interest, and if the minister went a little further and listened to another speech from the same hon. gentleman he might come back with some definite policy of debt reduction.
I submit further that the next budget should be a fair budget; it should not be a onesided budget. It should set forth our railway financing. Whether it is a debt on the country or whether it is not, it should be shown in the budget and not be hidden, leading us to believe that we are saving a lot of money and getting out of debt when as a matter of fact, according to the interpretation given by some of our financial position, we are not. These are some suggestions which I should like to see taken into account.
Again, between the address and the budget we should now have got down to some stated immigration policy. This government, since it has come into power, has had twenty immigration policies. And has it completed any one of them? What the policy is to-day no one knows. We are going along in a bog and fog and nobody knows. At one time we are told that no obstacle is placed in the way of our blood relations coming from Great Britain; but let one of these fellows offer to come here and he has to go to a great deal of trouble, answer a great many questions, fill in a number of forms, and pass medical examinations which in my opinion are an insult to the medical profession of Great Britain. It is an insult to them that we should send our medical men over there, as much as to say that they could not do the work properly. If the roster doctors whom we had before were given distinct instructions from the department, they could do the work. At any rate, there are still obstacles in the way to anyone from Great Britain who can pay his way to Canada.
I submit therefore, that we should have a well defined policy laid down by this government. But what have they done? We hear a lot about status, ambassadorial pilgrimages, appointments and so forth. But what have we in the way of a straight agricultural policy? The Minister of Agriculture made a very delightful trip over to France. May I tell him something in the way of economy as practised over there? I should like him to have looted over conditions in France. Had he done so he would have found that the Department of Agriculture in that country looks after its people. Wherever they find
[Mr. A. E. Ross.l
over-production in any commodity they immediately go into the raising of something else. It seems to me it is a good thing that the Prime Minister never put into practice to the full extent the promise he made this country that free potatoes would be brought in. What a calamity .that would have been to the province of the Postmaster General, where potatoes are selling to-day at thirty cents a bag. In France, had the minister studied the situation there, he would have found a department of agriculture which is an adviser and a parent to the agricultural people of that country, keeping them in touch with conditions, advising them what to raise and how to dispose of their surplus. But in this country there is no policy of any sort along the lines of agriculture.
On motion of Mr. Manaon the debate was adjourned.
